articles.titulo: An integrated One Health methodology to study Rift Valley fever, Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever and brucellosis at the human-livestock-wildlife interface in Uganda.
articles.autores: Kizito D, Tweed S, Mutyaba J, Babi N, Lule SA, Kiggundu GN, Gibb R, Nassuna CA, Ogwal RS, Paul E, Haumba M, Agaba C, Katushabe P, Enyel EM, Balinandi S, Franklinos L, Fuller N, Owen L, Ringwaldt E, Ferguson L, Ndumu DB, Sekamatte M, Atimnedi P, Nyakarahuka L, Kalema-Zikusoka G, Abubakar I, Field N, Seeley J, Lutwama JJ
articles.resumo_original: Zoonotic diseases pose a significant public health challenge, with most emerging diseases originating from animal populations. In Uganda, Rift Valley fever (RVF), Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF) and brucellosis are endemic, yet critical gaps remain in understanding their transmission dynamics, key vectors and reservoirs, environmental drivers, community knowledge and behaviours and the implementation of One Health policies. The Collaborative One Health Research Initiative on Epidemics-Uganda (COHRIE-Uganda) study developed an integrated, interdisciplinary approach to investigate these diseases across ecologically diverse areas characterised by intense human-livestock-wildlife interaction. The study methodology comprised sequential cross-sectional surveys combining quantitative and qualitative methods, involving community members, livestock, wildlife and vectors across six conservation areas in Uganda. Household surveys and blood sampling were obtained from 3018 individuals and 35 focus group discussions were conducted across 96 villages. 67 in-depth interviews with community leaders and 26 interviews with national policymakers were conducted to evaluate One Health policy implementation. Livestock practices were assessed through farmer questionnaires and blood sampling of 2199 cattle, 343 sheep, 78 pigs and 1582 goats. Invertebrate vector sampling was undertaken of 72,744 mosquitoes and 9273 ticks on livestock hosts with vertebrate host sampling of 612 small mammals. 233 large wildlife were sampled by blood and nasal swabs. Real-time monitoring and detection of zoonotic outbreaks was provided by 127 trained Community One Health Volunteers embedded at each site. COHRIE-Uganda presents a novel interdisciplinary methodology to study zoonotic disease, applying a One Health approach integrating molecular epidemiology, ecology, social sciences and community participatory methods involving humans, livestock, vectors, and wildlife to inform culturally sensitive zoonotic disease interventions.

articles.titulo: Establishing Potosi Virus as a Human Pathogen: Fatal Neuroinvasive Disease in a B-Cell-Depleted Patient.
articles.autores: Abbatemarco JR, Begum F, Villalba JA, Davis E, Bhatnagar J, Brault AC, Calvert AE, Chomyk A, Gould CV, Isada CM, Jung JU, Jones SE, Kang S, Ko Y, Li Y, Nakamura K, Najm L, Staples EJ, Trapp BD, Tipping P, Yeaney GA, Fox RJ
articles.resumo_original:
To establish Potosi virus, a mosquito-borne member of the family Peribunyaviridae, as a neuroinvasive human pathogen.
Case report.
A 37-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis on long-term rituximab developed rapidly progressive dementia. Serial MRI demonstrated progressive generalized atrophy. CSF showed transient, minimal lymphocytic pleocytosis. Extensive infectious, autoimmune, and prion evaluations were unrevealing, but CSF metagenomic sequencing detected all 3 genome segments for Potosi virus. Postmortem examination revealed diffuse meningoencephalitis with T-cell-predominant leptomeningeal and perivascular inflammation. Molecular analyses confirmed multiple nucleotide sequences with >99+% concordance with a known Potosi strain, with widespread viral infection confirmed by immunohistochemistry demonstrating intracellular and extracellular viral antigen. Electron microscopy demonstrated particles of a size consistent with the Peribunyaviridae family. Metagenomic sequencing of RNA extracted from frozen brain tissue identified all 3 Potosi virus gene segments without other infectious entities. Findings were concordant across multiple laboratories and institutions.
Potosi virus can cause fatal neuroinvasive disease in humans, as evidenced by convergent postmortem neuropathologic, molecular, and ultrastructural evidence. Chronic B-cell depletion may increase susceptibility to severe disease with arboviral infections, which may present without conventional CNS inflammatory markers. CSF metagenomic sequencing should be considered in immunocompromised patients with unexplained progressive neurologic decline.

articles.titulo: Assessing the Relative Contribution of Pre-Deployment Abroad Versus In-Mission Dirofilaria immitis Infections in French Military Working Dogs Screened Post-Mission: A Quantitative Risk Assessment.
articles.revista: Risk analysis : an official publication of the Society for Risk Analysis
articles.autores: Grosbois A, Risco-Castillo V, Watier-Grillot S, Crozet G
articles.resumo_original: Dirofilaria immitis (D. immitis) is a mosquito-borne nematode responsible for canine cardiopulmonary dirofilariasis, a parasitic infection widely distributed worldwide and established in mainland France, particularly in southern regions. Military working dogs (MWDs) may be at increased risk of exposure to vector-borne pathogens because of their predominantly outdoor lifestyle and frequent missions abroad. Nevertheless, D. immitis infection remains sporadic in this population, likely due to well-implemented medical prophylaxis. The aim of this study was to investigate the likely origin of D. immitis infections detected in MWD during post-mission screening using a quantitative risk analysis approach. Scenario trees were developed to describe the sequences of events leading to the return of an infected dog from a mission abroad, accounting for parasite biology, prophylactic measures, and compliance. The model estimated a mean annual number of 4.25 infected MWD returning from missions out of an average annual population of 466 returning dogs, of which 79% were detected through post-mission screening. Most infections were likely acquired before deployment, either during previous missions, at the breeding facility before purchase, or within mainland France. Only 7.9% of infections acquired during missions were expected to be detected by testing performed at the end of the post-mission quarantine period. Alternative scenarios highlighted the effectiveness of chemoprophylaxis, as its absence was associated with a 3.2-fold increase in the number of infected dogs. Simulations also showed that extending the interval between return and testing would substantially improve the detection of mission-acquired infections. These findings support the continued use of preventive measures while questioning the adequacy of current post-mission screening alone for identifying D. immitis infections acquired during deployment.

articles.titulo: Introduction and Spread of West Nile Virus in Lazio, Italy, 2025: Molecular Epidemiology and Genomic Characterization.
articles.autores: Rueca M, Gruber CEM, De Carli G, Mussetto I, Mavian CN, Manna G, Rosone F, La Rocca D, Perez-Jimenez JG, Scicluna MT, Chillemi G, Specchiarello E, Colavita F, Smoquina F, Nappo A, Merakou C, Sala MG, De Liberato C, Venturi G, Siddu A, Vairo F, Maggi F, Carletti F
articles.resumo_original: West Nile virus (WNV) is a flavivirus whose cycle involves mosquitoes and avian hosts that occasionally may infect horses and humans as "dead-end hosts." Human infection is mostly asymptomatic, sometimes leading to febrile or neuroinvasive disease. In 2025, Italy experienced its largest epidemic with an unprecedented geographic spread (79 provinces; 52% of cases in central Italy). Here we report whole‑genome sequencing and phylogeographic analysis of 39 WNV lineage 2 samples collected in Lazio and Campania regions between July and September 2025 from humans and animal samples. All 2025 strains belonged to a Southern Italian clade that diversified around 2020, with evidence of earlier circulation in 2024. All the 2025 genomes shared a substitution that lies in envelope protein domain III (K399R), potentially influencing interactions with the viral membrane. The same mutation was previously detected in Eastern European strains, leading to the hypothesis of introductions in Italy via migratory birds from these regions. Phylogeography identified strong viral dispersal routes within Central Italy supporting a pattern of short‑range spread and local overwintering. Overall, results highlight the roles of ecological conditions and cross‑border transmission dynamics in shaping the 2025 Italian epidemic, underscoring the need for integrated genomic/ecological surveillance.

articles.titulo: Epidemiological characteristics and transmission dynamics of dengue in Ningbo City, China before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic interventions.
articles.autores: Chu Y, Zhao Y, Abudunaibi B, Wang Y, Zhang Y, Lei S, Mao Y, He T, Chen T, Chen Y
articles.resumo_original:
Ningbo experienced a local dengue outbreak in 2018-2019, followed by the implementation and relaxation of COVID-19 pandemic interventions. Evidence has been limited on dengue epidemiology and the transmissibility across these periods.
We analyzed routine dengue cases and mosquito surveillance data from 2017 to 2024, using descriptive analyses to assess the epidemiological characteristics, and a mathematical model was developed to estimate the basic reproduction number (R0).
A total of 266 dengue cases were reported, with no deaths. Before the pandemic interventions, 51.19% of cases were overseas-imported; no cases were reported during pandemic interventions, whereas 73.47% were domestically imported after pandemic interventions. The median age of cases was 38.50 years (IQR = 31.25-54.00), and 57.52% were unemployed, retired, or in commercial services. The onset-to-diagnosis interval shortened post-interventions (4.46 days vs. 2.67 days). Viral typing increased post-interventions (34.59% vs. 63.27%), with 83.70% of cases identified as dengue virus-1 infections. Dengue cases were reported across all districts, with higher proportions in Haishu (27.07%) and Yinzhou (24.44%). The incidence was 2.82 per 100,000 persons. Incidence did not differ significantly by sex, but was significantly higher among individuals 15-59 years and those aged ≥60years than among those aged ≤14 years (3.18 and 3.01 per 100,000 persons, respectively, vs. 0.45 per 100,000 persons). Incidence was highest in Haishu and Jiangbei (6.90 and 4.93 per 100,000 persons, respectively). A post-intervention incidence rebound was observed, although no statistically significant differences were observed in the ≤ 14 age group, Beilun District, Ninghai County and Xiangshan County. Aedes albopictus was the only vector species. The mean Breteau Index was 16.07 (SD: 8.04) and decreased across phases, and rebounded in Jiangbei, Zhenhai, and Haishu districts. The mean BI was higher in summer compared to other seasons (p < 0.05). Model fit was strong (R2 > 0.95). The median R0 was higher in the outbreak years (3.46, IQR = 2.98-3.95) than years without local transmission (0.00, IQR = 0.00-0.00; p < 0.001). Median R0 was 0.00 (IQR = 0.00-0.71) over 2017-2024 due to the absence of local cases in most years.
Dengue remains non-endemic in Ningbo, and is driven primarily by imported infections rather than sustained local transmission. Despite a reduction in diagnostic delay and vector density, post-PHSM incidences rebounded, and district-level heterogeneity indicates ongoing outbreak potential. Sustained surveillance, rapid diagnosis and district-tailored vector control are critical to prevent re-establishment of local transmission.

articles.titulo: Functional dissection of conserved RNAi pathways in antiviral immunity of several hemipteran insects.
articles.autores: Zhang Y, Ye ZX, Ma QL, Wang BY, Zhuo JC, Huang HJ, Zhang CX, Chen JP, Li JM
articles.resumo_original: The small silencing RNA pathways are crucial post-transcriptional gene silencing mechanisms involved in antiviral defense, gene regulation, and transposon suppression. In insects, the three main pathways are the microRNA (miRNA), Piwi-interacting RNA (piRNA), and small interfering RNA (siRNA) pathways. While these pathways are well-studied in model insects like fruit flies and mosquitoes (Order: Diptera), their functions in non-model insects remain largely unexplored. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive functional screening of core RNAi-related genes in a hemipteran insect, the small brown planthopper (Laodelphax striatellus). Our results demonstrated that genes in the miRNA pathway (AGO1 and DCR1) and the piRNA pathway (Piwi and AGO3) are essential for the survival, development, and fecundity of L. striatellus, but they are not actively involved in the antiviral response. Unexpectedly, knocking down the key siRNA pathway gene DCR2 did not produce a detectable change in viral accumulation or the abundance of virus-derived small interfering RNAs. This finding suggests that substantial depletion of DCR2 does not detectably impair the measured antiviral siRNA responses in L. striatellus under our experimental conditions. A similar lack of detectable antiviral phenotypes following DCR2 knockdown was observed in three other representative hemipteran insects from different families/genera (Sogatella furcifera, Nilaparvata lugens, and Bemisia tabaci). Additionally, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of DCR2 resulted in embryonic lethality in homozygous mutant strains of L. striatellus, while heterozygous mutants showed significantly prolonged developmental duration. Functional RNAi-of-RNAi assays further demonstrated that DCR2 pre-knockdown did not detectably reduce silencing of a subsequently introduced dsRNA reporter in L. striatellus, and DCR2-heterozygous mutants with reduced DCR2 expression showed no change in viral accumulation. These results reveal an essential developmental role for DCR2 and indicate that partial DCR2 depletion does not measurably compromise antiviral immunity under the tested conditions. Collectively, our findings broaden our understanding of the organization and biological functions of small silencing RNA pathways in hemipteran insects.

articles.titulo: High quality chromosomal genome assemblies of three human Plasmodium species directly from natural infections.
articles.autores: Dogga SK, Rop JC, Makunin A, Teltscher F, Pointon DL, Sims Y, Uliano-Silva M, Torrance J, Mathers TC, Wood JMD, Sissoko S, Dara A, Ouologuem DT, Talman AM, Djimdé AA, Lawniczak MKN
articles.resumo_original: Malaria, caused by mosquito-transmitted Plasmodium parasites, remains a major global health challenge. While P. falciparum accounts for most malaria deaths, the lesser-studied P. ovale spp. and P. malariae also contribute to disease burden across many endemic regions, typically causing milder but chronic infections. Here, we generated high quality, chromosome-level reference genomes for P. ovale wallikeri, P. malariae, and P. falciparum directly from blood samples taken from natural infections. Using PacBio Ultra-Low-Input HiFi long-read sequencing and Hi-C chromatin conformation capture, we overcome limitations posed by low parasite biomass and the absence of in vitro culture for P. ovale wallikeri and P. malariae. These high quality reference genomes resolve previously inaccessible subtelomeric regions that include expanded gene families likely involved in host-parasite interactions, and they enhance our understanding of parasite persistence, transmission, immune evasion and comparative evolutionary studies. This work provides a critical foundation for including these neglected species in global malaria elimination efforts.

articles.titulo: Challenges and opportunities for strengthening South American responses to insecticide resistance in disease vectors: Lessons from the WINSA workshop in Bogotá, Colombia.
articles.autores: Martins AJ, Ahumada M, Bowman TS, Cabrera OL, Doerdjan-Ramoutar K, Dos Santos Dias L, Duchemin JB, Duchon S, Figueroa L, Flores AE, González CR, González-Brítez N, Harburguer L, Lenhart A, Lima JBP, Lopez R, Morales D, Quinones ML, Salcedo MP, Willat G, Corbel V
articles.resumo_original:
Vector-borne diseases remain a major and evolving public health challenge in South America, where arboviruses such as dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and malaria continue to expand in incidence and geographic distribution. Insecticides remain central to vector control programs; however, the rapid emergence and spread of insecticide resistance across multiple vector species increasingly threaten the effectiveness and sustainability of these interventions. In response to these challenges, the Worldwide Insecticide Resistance Network-South America (WINSA) organized a regional workshop in Bogotá, Colombia, in March 2026 to assess the current status of insecticide resistance, identify research priorities, and strengthen regional collaboration.
The workshop brought together experts from 13 South American countries and territories representing academia, public health institutions, and international organizations. Sixteen presentations addressed the current status of insecticide resistance in major disease vectors, including mosquitoes and triatomines. Discussions covered surveillance systems, resistance mechanisms, molecular and genomic tools, operational challenges, and innovative vector control strategies.
The workshop highlighted widespread resistance to pyrethroids and organophosphates across multiple vector species in South America. High frequencies of knockdown resistance mutations (kdr) and evidence of metabolic resistance mechanisms were reported in several countries, particularly in the dengue vector Aedes aegypti. Emerging resistance to novel insecticide formulations was also identified. Participants emphasized major disparities in surveillance capacity, insufficient standardization of methodologies, and uneven geographical coverage across the region. An Integrated Vector Resistance management framework, integrating biological, molecular, genomic, and spatial surveillance approaches, was proposed to support evidence-based decision-making in vector control. Innovative approaches, including insecticide combinations, spatial repellents, and insecticidal paints, were presented as promising complementary tools for integrated vector management.
Insecticide resistance represents a growing threat to the control of arboviral and malaria vectors in South America. Strengthening harmonized surveillance systems, integrating molecular and genomic tools, and improving regional coordination are critical priorities. WINSA provides a strategic scientific and technical platform to support collaborative research, capacity building, harmonized resistance surveillance, and the translation of resistance evidence into information that can support vector-control decision-making across the region.

articles.titulo: Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, cytotoxicity and larvicidal activities of Ziziphus oenopolia leaves: in vitro and in silico studies.
articles.autores: Ramalingam SV, Soloman VG, Bakthavatchalam S, Ramachandran K, Vinayagam R, Wen ZH, Govindasamy C, Almutairi KM, Lo YH
articles.resumo_original: The present study investigated the phytochemical composition, in vitro and in silico biological activities, and insecticidal properties of Ziziphus oenopolia (L) Mill. leaf extracts. The LC-MS profile of Ziziphus oenopolia leaves extract, which identified major phytochemical classes of fatty acids, flavonoids, and phenolic acids. The GC-MS profile, including n-hexadecanoic acid, phytol, and 9,12,15-octadecatrienoic acid, which were predicted by PASS and ADMET profiling to exhibit strong antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, cytotoxic, and larvicidal activities. The hydroalcoholic extract demonstrated the highest biological efficacy across multiple assays. In vitro antioxidant evaluation revealed strong DPPH and ABTS radical scavenging activities with IC₅₀ values of 41.04 and 43.54 µg/mL, respectively. The extract also showed significant protein anti-denaturation effects against bovine serum albumin and egg albumin (IC₅₀ = 315.53 and 311.60 µg/mL), significant cytotoxicity (EC₅₀ = 173.92 µg/mL), and strong larvicidal activity (LC₅₀ = 126.09 µg/mL for Aedes aegypti and 136.01 µg/mL for Tribolium castaneum), all exhibiting dose-dependent inhibition. In silico molecular docking further supported these findings, revealing strong binding affinities of the phytoconstituents toward human peroxiredoxin 5 as an antioxidant target, COX-2 (PDB: 1PXX) as an anti-inflammatory target, EGFR (PDB: 2EB3) as an anticancer target, and juvenile hormone binding protein (PDB: 5V13) as a larvicidal target. Overall, Z. oenopolia may contribute to the development of natural antioxidants and anti-inflammatory agents for mitigating oxidative stress-related and chronic inflammatory diseases.

articles.titulo: Oya virus reporter systems for high-throughput screening of viral replication inhibitors in mosquito cells.
articles.autores: Chen W, Xiong G, Ren N, Guo Y, Li X, Ma H, Huang D, Ghonaim AH, Wang J, Yuan Z, Wang F, Xia H
articles.resumo_original: Orthobunyaviruses are a diverse group of arboviruses, yet reporter virus-based inhibitor screening in mosquito-derived cells remains underexplored. Oya virus (OYAV), a Simbu serogroup orthobunyavirus detected in humans, mosquitoes, and midges, currently lacks reverse genetics tools and quantitative compound screening platforms. In this study, we established the first plasmid-based reverse genetics system for OYAV, successfully rescuing recombinant wild-type virus (rOYAV/WT) alongside fluorescent reporter viruses expressing enhanced green fluorescent protein (rOYAV/eGFP/S) or mCherry (rOYAV/mCherry/S). Both reporter viruses maintained stable reporter expression and infectivity across multiple vertebrate and mosquito-derived cell lines, although reporter insertion resulted in attenuated replication compared with the parental virus. Leveraging the robust fluorescence signal and retention of the reporter-containing region during serial passage, we developed a mosquito cell-based high-content screening platform to identify compounds inhibiting OYAV replication in C6/36 cells. The assay demonstrated high robustness and reproducibility, with a Z' factor of 0.755, and showed strong correlation with wild-type virus replication profiles. By screening an 800-compound library, we identified 10 candidates exhibiting >95% inhibitory activity against OYAV replication. Among these, saikosaponin B2, fingolimod (hydrochloride), and fangchinoline displayed micromolar inhibitory effects against both reporter and wild-type OYAV replication, with limited cytotoxicity in C6/36 cells. Collectively, this study establishes the reverse genetics system for OYAV and a quantitative mosquito-cell-based screening platform for orthobunyavirus replication inhibitors, providing a valuable tool for studying OYAV replication and evaluating antiviral compounds in mosquito-derived cells.IMPORTANCEOya virus (OYAV) is an emerging arbovirus circulating in Asia, with documented infection in humans and arthropod vectors. However, the absence of reverse genetics and reporter systems has limited mechanistic studies and inhibitor discovery for OYAV, particularly in arthropod-derived cells. Here, we established a reverse genetics system and generated fluorescent reporter viruses that enable real-time monitoring of OYAV replication. The optimized reporter virus was further used to establish a high-throughput inhibitor screening platform in mosquito C6/36 cells, leading to the identification of three compounds with inhibitory activity and low cytotoxicity in this system. These tools provide a foundation for investigating OYAV biology and facilitate the discovery and evaluation of inhibitors in vector cells and potentially in live vectors.

articles.titulo: Leptospirosis occurs as frequently as malaria among adolescent and adult acute febrile patients in Hoima, Uganda: A prospective health facility-based study.
articles.autores: Kirabo AV, Alinaitwe L, Kobba K, Ndawula EC, Ogwang J, Kirungi M, Ndagire A, Kankya C, Kakooza F, Lamorde M, Mayito J, Dreyfus A
articles.resumo_original:
Leptospirosis is underdiagnosed across sub-Saharan Africa, with its contribution to acute undifferentiated fever (AUF) poorly characterized. We determined the prevalence, risk factors, and clinical profile of leptospirosis among adolescents and adults with AUF at a referral hospital and health centre in Hoima, Uganda.
In a prospective health facility-based study with convalescent follow-up, blood and urine from AUF patients were tested by LipL32 real-time PCR (qPCR) and microscopic agglutination (MAT). Leptospirosis was confirmed by qPCR positivity, a single test MAT titre of ≥1:800, a fourfold titre rise or seroconversion (change from negative or 1:50 to ≥1:100 (lenient) or ≥1:200 (conservative)) in paired sera. Risk factors were identified by multivariable logistic regression.
Among 330 AUF patients, acute leptospirosis prevalence was 27.0% under the conservative definition (95% CI 22.3 to 32.1) and 32.7% under the lenient definition (95% CI 27.7 to 38.1). This was comparable to malaria at 30.3% (95% CI 25.3 to 35.3), and 8.8% of patients had both infections (95% CI 5.7 to 11.8). qPCR detected Leptospira DNA in 9.1% of patients. Agreement between qPCR and serology was low: 63.3% of qPCR-positive cases were confirmed by MAT, and only 24.4% of serologically confirmed cases were qPCR-positive. Seroprevalence (MAT titre 1:100 or above) was 35.8% (95% CI 30.6 to 41.2). L. interrogans serovar Bataviae was the predominant serovar, reported here for the first time in Uganda. Skinning animals (aOR 5.19, 95% CI 1.40 to 21.16) and mosquito exposure (aOR 2.31, 95% CI 1.17 to 4.70) were independent risk factors.
Leptospirosis occurs as frequently as malaria among AUF patients in Hoima warranting inclusion in Uganda's national febrile illness guidelines. The association of leptospirosis with skinning suggests a role of animal exposure in leptospirosis transmission. Poor qPCR-MAT concordance confirms that accurate case ascertainment requires combined molecular and serological diagnostics. While findings are regional, their implications are broader, highlighting the need to include zoonotic diseases in diagnosis and surveillance. Targeted treatment can reduce morbidity, mortality, and economic burden, while limiting antimicrobial resistance by decreasing broad-spectrum antibiotic use.

articles.titulo: Type III CI factors from wAlbB induce cytoplasmic incompatibility via a Host Modification mechanism.
articles.autores: Hou X, Goh FG, Liu S, Liu Y, Yong XE, Lin Q, Cai Y
articles.resumo_original: The widespread prevalence of the endosymbiotic bacterium Wolbachia among insect species relies on its ability to invade and manipulate host reproduction via several ways, among which cytoplasmic incompatibility (CI) is most studied. Two non-mutually exclusive models, the Host-Modification (HM) and the Toxin-Antidote (TA), have been proposed to explain the molecular basis of CI. Here, we investigate the CI-inducing activity of the Type III CI factors (cifs) from wAlbB, a strain currently being deployed to combat mosquito-borne diseases. This set of Cifs displays conserved subcellular localization dynamics in various insect cells. Both cifA and cifB are required for the induction of DNA damage in cultured cells, and transgenic Drosophila. Moreover, these cifs induce CI in Drosophila through the two-by-one manner, meaning cifA and cifB act together during spermatogenesis to induce CI, and maternal cifA can reverse the effect. Mechanistically, genetic, biochemical, cellular, and proteomic analyses reveal that this pair of cifs acts during the early stage of spermatogenesis but is dispensable in late-stage germline cells for CI induction. Collectively, our findings support the notion that wAlbB Type III cifs induce CI via a HM-based mechanism. Additional analyses suggest that different Wolbachia strains may employ distinct molecular mechanisms to induce CI.

articles.titulo: Natural Occurrence and Molecular Diversity of Wolbachia Endosymbiont DNA in Wild Mosquito Populations of Central India.
articles.revista: Vector borne and zoonotic diseases (Larchmont, N.Y.)
articles.autores: Khan N, Jain M, Mishra AK, Das A
articles.resumo_original:
Utilizing Wolbachia for mosquito biocontrol requires baseline understanding of natural infection dynamics, lineage diversity, and host-symbiont phylogenetic concordance across native vector populations.
We collected 2,167 adult mosquitoes (Anopheles, Culex, Aedes, and Mansonia) across five districts in central India (Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh). Specimens were screened in 263 genus-level pools via wsp PCR. Positive pools were brought to individuals level, typed across three different loci (ftsZ, gltA, and GroEL) of Wolbachia spp., and validated by mosquito barcoding (cox1, ITS2). Maximum likelihood phylogenies were constructed for all six loci both for Wolbachia (four) and mosquitoes (two).
Overall, 27 pools (10.26%) and 49 individuals (21.21%) were wsp-positive that includes 17 Anopheles, 18 Culex, 9 Aedes, and 5 Mansonia. Culicines exhibited robust multilocus amplification, whereas all 17 Anopheles failed to amplify at ftsZ, gltA, and GroEL. Phylogenetic trees of the mosquito-host cox1 and ITS2 resolved all four genera and five wsp-positive Anopheles species into monophyletic clades with 84-100% bootstrap support. In Wolbachia phylogenies, culicine isolates clustered in Supergroup B (wPip), with ftsZ and gltA trees resolving Mansonia symbionts into a well-supported, distinct lineage (95-97% bootstrap). Crucially, the wsp tree revealed that four An. annularis sequences formed a monophyletic clade (89-98% bootstrap), clustering with the bat-fly endosymbiont Penicillidia jenynsii rather than mosquito-adapted strains. Primary malaria vectors (An. culicifacies and An. fluviatilis) tested negative for Wolbachia.
Phylogenetic divergence and housekeeping gene dropout indicate that wsp detection in wild Anopheles represents transient or horizontal acquisition rather than stable intracellular endosymbiosis. Multilocus phylogenetic validation is critical prior to deploying symbiont-based biocontrol.

articles.titulo: Larvicidal activity of Zanthoxylum oxyphyllum Edgew. extract against Culex pipiens.
articles.revista: Journal of environmental science and health. Part. B, Pesticides, food contaminants, and agricultural wastes
articles.autores: Zoramthara K, Manngaihsiam R, Sarmah MP, Boro HH, Vanlalmuanpuii K, Mongku M, Morajkar A, Kharat KR
articles.resumo_original: The increasing incidence of synthetic pesticide resistance in Culex pipiens, a principal vector for lymphatic filariasis, demands the immediate advancement of sustainable mosquitocides. This current research shows the larvicidal effectiveness, molecular processes, and environmental safety of the plant extract Zanthoxylum oxyphyllum (ZOM). Metabolite profiling using Liquid Chromatography-Tandem Mass Spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) showed the presence of flavonoid glycosides such as fortunellin and linarin, phenolic derivatives, and nitrogenous metabolites. ZOM showed larvicidal action against day-2 third-instar C. pipiens that depended on the dose and the period. The LC50 and LC90 values decreased from 43.14 (30.78-60.45) ppm and 132.46 (94.52-185.65) ppm at 12 h to 36.16 (26.06-50.16) ppm and 99.163 (71.48-137.56) ppm at 24 h, which showed that the activity of the treatment increased with time. Compared to untreated controls, ZOM-treated larvae had lower levels of both alkaline phosphatase (0.03797 vs. 0.00282 U mg-1 protein) and acetylcholinesterase (0.00396 vs. 0.00153 U mg-1 protein) activity. Standardized acute toxicity testing, as per OECD 2025 recommendations, aids in showing that ZOM does not harm the non-target indicator species Danio rerio. These results may confirm that ZOM is an effective, target-specific, and environmentally acceptable option for sustainable vector control programs against mosquitoes.

articles.titulo: Abundance and species diversity of mosquitoes (Diptera, Culicidae) in endemic areas for arboviruses in the Eastern Amazon, Brazil.
articles.autores: David EDS, Komninakis SV, da Silva LL, Fonseca EDC, Dos Santos KC, Barbosa LMC, Souto RNP
articles.resumo_original: Combating the spread of arboviruses in the Amazon relies on understanding the diversity of Culicidae, particularly potential vectors. Areas with historical records of vector occurrence provide crucial insights into the factors driving epidemic emergence. Furthermore, anthropogenic activities, such as deforestation and demographic pressure on the forest, are considered the primary drivers of new outbreaks, creating a scenario of high ecological receptivity for pathogens of public health concern. This study aimed to estimate mosquito richness and abundance in arbovirus-endemic areas within the districts of Carvão and Mazagão Velho, in the municipality of Mazagão, Amapá, Eastern Amazon. Four Culicidae sampling sites were established in each locality, utilizing CDC light traps and Human Landing Catch (HLC). Sampling campaigns began in January 2024 and concluded in December 2024, spanning both the rainy and less rainy seasons of the Amazon region. Specimens were identified at the Arthropoda Laboratory of the Federal University of Amapá. This research documented a total of 3.671 adult mosquitoes from the Culicidae family, encompassing 35 different species across 11 distinct genera. Only four genera are not considered arbovirus vectors in humans. The remaining genera include species of medical and epidemiological importance in arbovirus transmission, including species from the genera Anopheles, Aedes, Psorophora, Haemagogus, Culex, Coquillettidia and Mansonia. Environmental conditions favour high ecological receptivity for potential vectors, indicating a need for entomological surveillance near the study areas. Understanding the diversity of Culicidae reveals the importance of vector control in combating mosquito-borne pathogens in the Amazon.

articles.titulo: Controlled human infection with Plasmodium falciparum-infected mosquito bites elicits antibodies against mosquito salivary protein SG1L3.
articles.autores: Andrade CM, van Daalen RC, Fabra-García A, Grievink S, van Gemert GJ, Teelen K, Hester SS, Stoter R, van de Vegte-Bolmer M, Drakeley C, Tiono AB, Sauerwein RW, Bousema T, Jore MM
articles.resumo_original: Human malaria infections begin with the injection of Plasmodium sporozoites via mosquito saliva. Whole sporozoite immunizations have been used as a model to study immune responses to malaria parasites, having culminated in circumsporozoite protein (CSP)-targeting vaccines and monoclonal antibodies (mAbs). However, antibody responses targeting non-CSP antigens on the sporozoite surface remain poorly characterized. Here, we isolated single B cells from a human volunteer immunized by Plasmodium falciparum-infected mosquito bites, who had acquired non-CSP-specific antibodies that recognize sporozoites. We identified two mAbs that recognize the surface of P. falciparum sporozoites, but do not bind to CSP. Using immunoprecipitation followed by mass-spectrometry, we found that the target of these mAbs is not a P. falciparum protein but the mosquito salivary protein SG1L3. We observed that recombinant SG1L3 binds to P. falciparum sporozoites. However, the SG1L3-specific mAbs and SG1L3-specific polyclonal antibodies from this volunteer, as well as polyclonal antibodies raised against recombinant SG1L3 in rabbits, fail to block liver stage infection in vitro, making this an unlikely target for functional antibodies. We observed that inhabitants from an area with intense Anopheles exposure in Burkina Faso can have antibodies against SG1L3, and that antibody titers increase with age. In conclusion, we identified the first human mAbs against a mosquito saliva protein that binds to the surface of sporozoites. Future work should assess whether naturally acquired antibodies against this protein may be used as a serological marker of mosquito exposure.

articles.titulo: Patterns of insecticide resistance in Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus in different cities across Cameroon.
articles.autores: Djiappi-Tchamen B, Djapoum Theno C, Nana-Ndjangwo S, Mavridis K, Balaska S, Talipouo A, Joko S, Djamouko-Djonkam L, Bamou R, Mayi AMP, Kamgang B, Awono-Ambéné P, Dadji GAF, Vontas J, Antonio-Nkondjio C
articles.resumo_original: The increasing frequency of arboviral diseases' outbreaks in Cameroon necessitates evidence-based vector control. However, the efficacy of chemical control interventions is seriously threatened by the rapid evolution of insecticide resistance in Aedes vector populations. This study investigated the insecticide resistance profiles of Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus across ecologically diverse cities in Cameroon. Aedes larvae were collected from April to November 2024 in eight major cities representing diverse ecological landscapes across Cameroon: Yaoundé (Congo-Guinean equatorial forest); Douala and Kribi (coastal areas); Nkongsamba, Bafoussam, Mbouda, and Maroua (highland areas); and Bertoua (sub-tropical/savanna transition zone). World Health Organization (WHO) insecticide susceptibility bioassays were conducted on F1 adults against pyrethroids (0.75% permethrin, 0.05% deltamethrin), carbamates (0.1% propoxur, 0.1% bendiocarb), and organophosphates (0.05% pirimiphos-methyl). Molecular mechanisms potentially driving insecticide resistance were characterized using multiplex TaqMan qPCR to genotype kdr mutations and RT-qPCR to quantify the expression of detoxification genes such as cytochrome P450s, Glutathione S-transferases, and Carboxylesterases. Ae. aegypti displayed widespread resistance to pyrethroids, with mortality as low as 17.4% (permethrin, Kribi). This resistance could possibly be attributed to distinct geographic distribution of target-site mutations, with F1534C ranging from absent in Bafoussam to 95% in Kribi and Bertoua (alongside high frequencies in Yaoundé and Douala), and V1016I peaking at 46.3% in Bertoua while remaining absent in Bafoussam and Maroua. Furthermore, double-mutant homozygous haplotypes (CC-II) reached up to 15%, alongside massive metabolic upregulation, notably a 184.8-fold increase in GSTD4 expression in Bafoussam. In contrast, Ae albopictus populations appeared generally more susceptible across most sites, though localized resistance to permethrin and deltamethrin emerged in Douala and Nkongsamba. Susceptibility to bendiocarb and pirimiphos-methyl was observed across all sites for both species. In contrast, most of these populations were found to be resistant to propoxur. The continued susceptibility of Ae. albopictus in most regions, contrasted with its emerging resistance in urban centers, underscores the need for species-specific and geographically tailored management interventions. Overall, these findings emphasize the urgent need to deploy targeted larviciding approaches in breeding sites and integrate routine resistance monitoring to mitigate the spread of arboviral vectors across Cameroon.

articles.titulo: Paperclip RNAs bypass clathrin mediated endocytosis in insect and fungal cells.
articles.autores: Amanat N, Kernodle BM, Castillo B, Tayler A, Belmonte M, Whyard S
articles.resumo_original: Insects and fungi are among the most destructive pests and pathogens affecting agriculture and public health. Although chemical pesticides have long been the primary means of control, their broad‑spectrum activity and widespread use have accelerated resistance in many systems. RNA interference (RNAi) has therefore emerged as a promising species‑specific alternative. RNAi is initiated by double‑stranded RNA (dsRNA), which triggers sequence‑directed degradation of target transcripts. However, RNAi efficiency varies markedly across species, influenced by nuclease activity, dsRNA length, and the cellular uptake route. We previously showed that long dsRNA uptake in Aedes aegypti depends on clathrin‑mediated endocytosis (CME), whereas paperclip RNA (pcRNA), a compact dsRNA structure developed in our laboratory, bypasses CME and enters cells through a distinct pathway. Here, we compared the uptake and RNAi performance of two dsRNA formats, long dsRNA (210-230 bp) and pcRNA (21-23 bp), in three representative species: Aedes aegypti (mosquito), Spodoptera frugiperda (moth), and Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (fungus). To assess cellular uptake of these dsRNAs, we used two CME inhibitors, chlorpromazine (CPZ) and bafilomycin A1 (BafA1), along with fluorescein‑labeled dsRNAs. CME inhibition prevented long dsRNA from entering the cytoplasm and abolished its ability to induce RNAi. In contrast, pcRNAs were readily internalized and produced significant gene knockdowns under both inhibitor treatments. Microscopy further revealed that all three cell types, pretreated with either CPZ or BafA1, prevented long dsRNA from entering the cytoplasm. pcRNA, consistently reached the cytoplasm and showed superior uptake across all species. Together, these findings demonstrate that pcRNA uses an uptake mechanism distinct from long dsRNA, enabling it to circumvent CME-dependent barriers. This unique internalization route likely reflects its compact size and structural configuration and highlights pcRNA as a promising platform for improving RNAi-based pest and pathogen control.

articles.titulo: Conditional genetic manipulation systems in mosquitoes: Progress, Challenges, and perspectives.
articles.autores: Ma J, Bai XY, Ling X, Xie XY, Xu Y, Cai X, Wu LY, Xie YX, Yang CZ, Li M, Qiao L
articles.resumo_original: Mosquitoes are major vectors of severe infectious diseases, including malaria, dengue fever, and chikungunya, and continue to pose a substantial threat to global public health. A comprehensive understanding of mosquito-pathogen interactions, disease transmission mechanisms, and ecological adaptations is essential for developing innovative strategies to control mosquito-borne diseases. In recent years, genetic manipulation technologies have greatly advanced functional genomics research in mosquitoes; however, their limited spatiotemporal precision restricts the functional characterization of essential genes, key developmental regulators, and tissue-specific genes, often due to embryonic or early developmental lethality, systemic editing effects, and complex phenotypic consequences. As an important strategy for precision genetic regulation, Conditional Genetic Manipulation Systems (CGMSs) utilize tissue-specific, developmental stage-specific, or externally inducible regulatory elements to achieve controlled expression of functional genetic components (e.g., Cas9), thereby enabling spatiotemporally precise genetic modifications. These systems provide a new research paradigm for investigating mosquito basic biology and developing genetic control technologies. This review systematically summarizes the major types, regulatory mechanisms, and current advances of CGMSs in mosquitoes, with particular emphasis on different regulatory elements and their applications in functional gene analysis, studies of pathogen transmission mechanisms, and vector control strategies. Furthermore, we discuss future directions for expanding editing systems and developing genetic manipulation resources, aiming to provide insights into the construction of precise genetic manipulation systems in mosquitoes and other insects and the advancement of next-generation genetic control technologies.

articles.titulo: Assessing dengue vector breeding in diverse environments for targeted interventions: Case studies from Colombia and Nepal.
articles.revista: Current research in parasitology & vector-borne diseases
articles.autores: Barahona E, Nelson-Cofie D, Kroeger A, Chavarría K, Vence N, Banjara MR
articles.resumo_original: Dengue and other Aedes-borne diseases are increasing globally, with vector control being the primary prevention strategy in the absence of an effective vaccine. Because mosquitoes breed in domestic water containers, identifying the most productive container types is essential for targeted interventions. This study compared pupal productivity of Aedes spp. and productive container types in two settings in Colombia and Nepal with distinct environmental, epidemiological, and water storage characteristics. A pupal/demographic survey was conducted in Valledupar, Colombia, and Triyuga Municipality, Nepal, including 300 and 121 households, respectively. Pupal counts were used as a proxy for adult mosquito production. In Colombia, 16 of 506 containers were productive, with large water storage containers accounting for over 90% of pupae. In Nepal, 34 of 396 containers were productive, with containers such as barrels and flower vases contributing most pupae. In both locations, pupal production was highly clustered in a small number of containers. These findings show that the most productive breeding sites differ between places, with large containers dominating in Colombia and smaller containers in Nepal. Targeted vector control strategies should therefore, focus on the specific container types responsible for most pupal production in each context. Context-specific interventions guided by pupal/demographic surveys are essential for efficient dengue control.

articles.titulo: Household environmental management practices, community engagement, and self-reported malaria incidence in urban and rural communities of Malawi.
articles.autores: Lungu MM, Davitadze A
articles.resumo_original: Malaria control in Malawi relies primarily on long-lasting insecticide-treated nets (LLITNs) and indoor residual spraying (IRS), but transmission remains heterogeneous across districts. Previous research indicates that community-based environmental management strategies, such as routine drainage maintenance, vegetation removal, and effective household waste disposal, may reduce environmental conditions conducive to malaria vector proliferation. This study investigated the association between environmental management practices at both household and community levels and self-reported cases of malaria in Malawi. We disseminated an online survey through social media from December 2024 to February 2025, targeting adults in both rural and urban locales, resulting in 282 participants. Negative binomial regression was employed to assess the relationship between preventive measures, household-level environmental management practices, community engagement, and malaria cases during the past year. LLITNs were the most used preventive measure (62.1%). Their use was significantly associated with fewer malaria cases in rural areas (p = 0.035) but more malaria cases in urban areas (p = 0.018). Household-level (94.3%) and community-level (70.9%) environmental management practices were widely reported but showed weak and area-dependent associations with malaria incidence. Regardless of area of residence, respondents faced difficulties maintaining these practices, mostly due to time constraints (49.3%) and financial constraints (61.3%). Strengthening community education, resource support, and integration of environmental management into existing programs is likely to be needed to sustain these practices. The contrasting rural-urban patterns may reflect unmeasured differences in local transmission intensity and warrant investigation in studies with geographically resolved data.

articles.titulo: Identification of Usutu virus in blood donors as part of molecular screening for West Nile virus, France, 2023.
articles.revista: Euro surveillance : bulletin Europeen sur les maladies transmissibles = European communicable disease bulletin
articles.autores: Gallian P, Grard G, Le Cam S, Klitting R, Guillet M, Barlet V, Lacoste M, Ricard C, Brisbarre N, Isnard C, Pezzi L, Ayhan N, Piorkowski G, Amaral R, Peyrard T, Paty MC, Franke F, Laperche S, Durand GA, de Lamballerie X
articles.resumo_original: BACKGROUNDWest Nile Virus (WNV) can be transmitted via blood transfusion and lead to neuroinvasive forms in recipients of blood products.AIMWe aimed to investigate WNV and Usutu virus (USUV) infections among blood donors in France.METHODSBlood donations in 18 of 96 departments of metropolitan France and from travellers returning from affected areas were screened prospectively for WNV using a commercial nucleic acid test (NAT). In addition, stored samples from blood donations in the affected departments were retrospectively tested with RT-qPCR. Differentiation between WNV and USUV infections in NAT-positive samples was done with a RT-qPCR or by seroneutralisation after seroconversion.RESULTSBetween 18 July and 1 December 2023, 34 (0.018%) of 185,965 blood donation samples were initially positive for WNV. After investigations, 20 donors with USUV infections (16 confirmed, four probable) and five with WNV infections (three confirmed, two probable) were identified. In samples from four donors, WNV and USUV could not be differentiated, and five samples remained indeterminate. Seventeen USUV infections were considered autochthonous: nine departments in the southern and central parts of France, including two departments where WNV was also detected. Infections with USUV were detected between 21 July and 17 October and WNV between 23 August and 20 September.CONCLUSIONVia screening of blood donations, we could identify the circulation of USUV in 2023 in large parts of metropolitan France. A One Health approach is required to better understand the determinants of USUV circulation in France and the clinical consequences of USUV infections in humans.

articles.titulo: Malaria and associated factors after RTS,S/AS01 vaccination in children in Komenda-Edina-Eguafo-Abrem Municipality, Ghana: A facility-based cross-sectional study.
articles.revista: The Journal of international medical research
articles.autores: Aninagyei E, Boatey CA, Musah S, Danzo KF, Corley JS, Tanson KS, Zilevu G
articles.resumo_original: ObjectiveMalaria remains a major public health challenge in Ghana despite the implementation of multiple control measures, including the RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix) malaria vaccine. This study assessed malaria rapid diagnostic test positivity and associated factors among individuals presenting with suspected malaria in the Komenda-Edina-Eguafo-Abrem District, Ghana.MethodsThis facility-based cross-sectional study included 400 individuals of all age groups who presented with suspected malaria at the Salvation Army Hospital, Ajumako Ba. Malaria was diagnosed using rapid diagnostic tests. Data on sociodemographic characteristics, malaria control practices, environmental exposures, and vaccination status were collected using structured questionnaires. Associations were assessed using chi-square tests and binary logistic regression to identify independent predictors of malaria infection.ResultsThe overall malaria rapid diagnostic test positivity rate was 20.8% (83/400). Malaria test positivity differed significantly by age (p < 0.001), with the highest burden observed among children and adolescents. Sleeping under a mosquito net the preceding night was strongly protective (adjusted odds ratio = 0.17, 95% confidence interval: 0.07-0.40, p < 0.001). In contrast, sharing mosquito nets with one person (adjusted odds ratio = 4.51, 95% confidence interval: 1.31-15.50, p = 0.02), with more than one person (adjusted odds ratio = 4.76, 95% confidence interval: 0.92-24.47, p = 0.06), prolonged nocturnal outdoor activity (adjusted odds ratio = 4.49, 95% confidence interval: 1.44-14.03, p = 0.01), and proximity to gullies or stagnant water (adjusted odds ratio = 2.49, 95% confidence interval: 1.24-5.01, p = 0.01) significantly increased malaria risk. Among children younger than 7 years, malaria prevalence was lower in RTS,S/AS01-vaccinated children (29.6%) compared to unvaccinated children (60%), although differences were not statistically significant overall. Significant associations in this age group were observed with mosquito net use, nocturnal outdoor activity, and nearby vegetation.ConclusionMalaria rapid diagnostic test positivity remains high in the Komenda-Edina-Eguafo-Abrem Municipality, particularly among children. Mosquito net use, nocturnal outdoor activity, and proximity to potential mosquito breeding sites were associated with rapid diagnostic test positivity. The small vaccine-eligible subgroup limited conclusions on RTS,S/AS01 vaccination. Integrated, community-based malaria control strategies remain essential for sustained reductions in malaria transmission.

articles.titulo: First record of Culex (Culex) acharistus Root, 1927 (Diptera: Culicidae) in Bolivia: morphological and molecular confirmation across contrasting Andean environments.
articles.autores: Lardeux F, Boussès P, Quezada C, Berger A, Lardeux R, Aliaga C, Torrez L
articles.resumo_original: This study reports the first record of Culex (Culex) acharistus Root, 1927 in Bolivia, based on an integrative approach combining larval morphology and molecular identification using a fragment of the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) gene. Specimens were collected from 4 localities representing contrasting environmental settings: La Paz (urban environment, approximately 3,600 m a.s.l.), El Alto (urban environment, approximately 4,000 m a.s.l.), Cochabamba (urban and peri-urban environments, approximately 2,600 m a.s.l.), and Licoma, a rural locality in the Yungas region (approximately 1,900 m a.s.l.). Fourth-instar larvae were morphologically examined using diagnostic characters and preserved for molecular analyses. The 6 analyzed specimens shared an identical COI haplotype, showing more than 99% sequence identity with available Cx. acharistus sequences in GenBank. Maximum likelihood phylogenetic analysis placed the Bolivian haplotype within the Cx. acharistus clade. These results provide morphological and molecular evidence for the occurrence of Cx. acharistus in Bolivia, extend its known distribution in South America, and document the species at its highest elevation reported to date, at approximately 4,000 m a.s.l. in El Alto. This study highlights the value of integrating morphological and molecular approaches for reliable identification of Neotropical Culex species.

articles.titulo: Preliminary case study of vertical distribution and trap efficiency of Aedes (Diptera: Culicidae) mosquitoes in urban multi-storey buildings in Selangor, Malaysia.
articles.autores: Zurkarnain MA, Rahman MA, Othman H, Hod R, Hassan MR, Sulistiyani S, Agustar HK
articles.resumo_original: The increasing prevalence of high-rise residential developments in dengue-endemic regions has created new challenges for understanding the distribution and surveillance of Aedes mosquitoes. This study investigated the vertical distribution of Aedes mosquitoes and evaluated the effectiveness of two modified low-cost sticky trap designs in a high-rise residential complex in Hulu Langat, Selangor, Malaysia. A total of 108 sticky traps comprising small and large trap designs were deployed across multiple floor levels in two residential blocks over four sampling rounds. Adult mosquitoes were identified morphologically, and trap performance was assessed using sticky trap indices and Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) analysis. Aedes aegypti was the dominant species captured throughout the study, particularly in Block A, whereas Ae. albopictus was more frequently detected in Block B. Adult Aedes mosquitoes were recorded from lower parking levels to the highest residential floors, demonstrating extensive vertical distribution within the building environment. Large sticky traps consistently outperformed small traps, recording higher sticky trap indices, greater mosquito captures, and all mixed-species detections. Negative-binomial GEE indicated that floor level and trap size were significant predictors of Ae. aegypti abundance, while binary logistic regression showed that the probability of Ae. aegypti detection also increased with floor level and was substantially higher in large traps. These findings demonstrate that Aedes mosquitoes are capable of occupying a wide vertical range in high-rise residential buildings and highlight the value of low-cost stiky traps as practical surveillance tools. The study provides important ecological insights into urban mosquito distribution and supports the development of scalable surveillance strategies for dengue vector management in increasingly vertical urban landscapes.

articles.titulo: Molecular and functional characterization of a typical 2-Cys peroxiredoxin and its developmental and pyriproxyfen-responsive expression in Aedes albopictus (Diptera: Culicidae).
articles.autores: Arslanhan BA, Diop SD, Sahin S, Toroslu AM, Kizgin AD, Pekmezci GZ, Inci A, Yildirim A
articles.resumo_original: The Asian tiger mosquito, Aedes albopictus (Skuse, 1894) (Diptera: Culicidae), is established and expanding across the Black Sea region, but the redox processes associated with its development and response to insect growth regulators remain poorly understood. We characterized a typical 2-Cys peroxiredoxin (Prx2) by examining intraspecific sequence variation, conserved protein features, enzymatic activity, developmental transcription, and transcription following exposure to 0.06 ppb pyriproxyfen. The coding region was polymorphic among Turkish isolates, but all substitutions were synonymous, and the deduced amino acid sequence was conserved. Catalytic cysteines and hallmark motifs supported classification as a typical 2-Cys peroxiredoxin. Recombinant His-tagged Prx2 migrated at the expected molecular size and removed hydrogen peroxide in a concentration- and thiol-dependent manner. Basal transcript abundance varied across development, reaching its lowest level in pupae and higher levels in adults. Exposure to 0.06 ppb pyriproxyfen was associated with increased Prx2 transcript abundance in L3 and L4 larvae, whereas no statistically detectable treatment-related difference was observed among the surviving pupae or adults at the sampled time points. Together, these findings identify Prx2 as a conserved, functional thiol peroxidase and demonstrate a pyriproxyfen-associated larval transcriptional response under the conditions tested. Because this concentration was not independently validated as sublethal in the present colony and later-stage sampling necessarily comprised survivors of the original exposure, the data do not distinguish developmental attenuation of the response from survivor selection.

articles.titulo: The hidden malaria: misidentification of Plasmodium malariae and Plasmodium ovale in low-transmission setting targeted for elimination in Ethiopia.
articles.autores: Getachew H, Wang C, Habtamu K, Demissew A, Degefa T, Birhanie SK, Kazura JW, King CL, Yan G, Yewhalaw D
articles.resumo_original:
Quartan malaria caused by Plasmodium malariae (Pm) and tertian Plasmodium ovale (Po) malaria has been largely overlooked in Ethiopia due to their milder clinical symptoms, lower prevalence, and frequently misdiagnosis during routine microscopic. This study estimated the prevalence of Pm and Po infections misdiagnosed as P. vivax (Pv) in selected health facilities in southwestern Ethiopia.
A cross-sectional study was conducted among study participants who were positive for Pv by microscopy or rapid diagnostic test (RDT) and who were attending health facilities within Arjo-Didessa sugarcane plantations and surrounding areas in Oromia, southwestern Ethiopia, between September 2019 and July 2022. Of the 3590 febrile patients attending health facilities, 323 were Pv positive by microscopy or RDT. Among these, 245 Pv-positive samples were re-evaluated using quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR). Species-specific primers targeting Pv, P. falciparum (Pf), Pm, and Po were used for species confirmation.
From 245 vivax malaria cases, RDT were performed to 162 sub-samples, among them 8.6% (14/162) were negative by RDT. None of the samples tested by RDT and microscopy detected Pm or Po. Of these 245 tested and reported as Pv positive by microscopy, qPCR confirmed that 215 (87.7%, 95% CI 82.98-91.58) were positive for Pv, 9 (3.7%, 95% CI 1.69-6.86) for Pf, 8 (3.3%, 95% CI 1.42-6.33) for Pm, 6 (2.4%, 95% CI 0.90-5.25) were positive for Po, and 7 (2.8%, 95% CI 1.16-5.80) had mixed infections (Pf and Pv).
The findings of this study highlights the need for a strategic shift to integrate Pm and Po into Ethiopia's malaria control and elimination program. Moreover, strengthening the diagnostic capacity should include training of microscopists for accurate Plasmodium species identification and adopting highly sensitive diagnostic tool for all four Plasmodium species in resource-limited settings. This is essential for enhancing malaria control and accelerating progress toward elimination.

articles.titulo: Cost comparison of community-based vector surveillance using VectorCamTM, an AI-enabled mosquito identification tool, versus routine entomological surveillance in Uganda.
articles.autores: Rincon Torroella M, Raman S, Patenaude BN, Patel S, Shodhan A, Zacharias A, Kansiime W, Maiteki C, Opigo J, Waiswa P, Acharya S
articles.resumo_original:
National malaria elimination programs depend on timely and reliable vector surveillance data to guide interventions. Current systems rely on analog data collection and microscopy-based morphological identification of mosquitoes by entomologists (vector control officers, VCO), a process constrained by limited entomologists, high specimen volumes, and specimen transport from rural collection sites. VectorCamTM is a smartphone-based device that uses AI to classify mosquito species, sex, and abdominal status within seconds, enabling automated workflows and the task-shifting of some entomologist responsibilities to community health workers (CHWs) or village health teams (VHTs). This study evaluated the unit cost of integrating VectorCamTM into routine surveillance in Uganda.
Data were extracted from a 12-month pragmatic parallel randomized trial conducted across two districts in Uganda from 2023 to 2024. This analysis accounted only for costs directly associated with field activities, including personnel, transport, and supplies. Three VectorCamTM implementation models were analyzed. Implementation Model 1 represented full task-shifting of mosquito surveillance responsibilities to village health teams, where they were collected, analyzed, mosquito identified and reported data without the involvement of VCO and the use of VectorCamTM. Implementation Model 2 incorporated quarterly supervision by VCO to support village health team-led activities. Implementation Model 3 included monthly VCO supervision, aligning with routine surveillance workflows, to assess the cost implications of adding digital surveillance to existing protocols.
The annual cost of routine surveillance (control arm) per district was USD $10,615. In comparison, VectorCamTM reduced costs to USD $8,852 in Model 1 (16.6% savings), USD $9,200 in Model 2 (13.3 savings), and USD $9896 in Model 3 (6.8% savings). These reductions were driven primarily by reductions in personnel and transport expenditures, although they were partially offset by higher supply costs associated with devices and service fees. The per-device analysis demonstrated that each VectorCamTM unit represented an annual cost of USD 144.51 but replaced USD 438.29 worth of surveillance functions, resulting in net savings of USD 293.78 per device under Implementation Model 1. Sensitivity analyses demonstrated increased savings in scenarios with existing digital infrastructure or the individual usage of VectorCamTM by one VHT.
Digitalizing vector surveillance with VectorCamTM offers a cost-saving and scalable approach for low- and middle-income countries. By shifting resources from specialized, labor-intensive methods such as microscopy to technology operable by CHW. VectorCamTM supports more efficient data collection while reducing costs. These findings suggest that integrating digital task-shifting tools into national malaria surveillance programs can enhance vector surveillance in resource-constrained settings.

articles.titulo: Anopheles larval ecology and physicochemical characterization of larval habitats in Dire Dawa: an area colonized by Anopheles stephensi in Eastern Ethiopia.
articles.autores: Abiy E, Degefa T, Balkew M, Merga H, Zewdu D, Ayala A, Atieli H, Lee MC, Zhou G, Yan G, Yewhalaw D
articles.resumo_original:
Understanding mosquito larval ecology is crucial for effective vector control strategies. While much is known about Anopheles larval habitat distribution, the impact of landscape (urban vs. rural) on Anopheles stephensi larval distribution and population dynamics in Ethiopia remains unclear.
A longitudinal study was conducted from February 2023 to December 2024 in aquatic habitats in urban, peri-urban, and rural areas of Dire Dawa City Administration, eastern Ethiopia. Mosquito larvae and pupae were collected and reared in a field insectary until adult emergence. The female Anopheles were morphologically identified and further confirmed via polymerase chain reaction (PCR). The physicochemical parameters of the larval habitats were measured via a HANNA multiparameter water probe. Statistical analyses included general linear models, ANOVA, logistic regression, paired sample t tests, chi-square tests, principal component analysis and correlation analyses to assess larval presence, density, and distribution in relation to water physicochemical parameters across the three ecological settings.
A total of 23,526 larvae and 1808 pupae of Anopheles mosquitoes were collected from 856 man-made habitats (bricks, plastic sheets, steel drums, tire tracks, canal ditches, and barrels) and 53 natural habitats (river edges, animal hoof prints, ponds, and swamps) in urban, peri-urban, and rural areas. Uncovered cemented cisterns were the main human-made larval habitats; river edges were the main natural habitats. Anopheles larvae were absent in the steel drums and plastic barrels at the rural sites. Anopheles larval density significantly differed across the different ecological settings (F = 7.8, df = 1, 908, p = 0.005) and among the different larval habitat types (F = 326.2, df = 1, 907, p < 0.001). Among the 2934 reared adults, 74.8% (2194/2934) were An. stephensi, 21.7% (636/2934) were An. arabiensis, and 3.0% were other species (An. pharoensis, An. coustani, An. amharicus, An. pretoriensis). An. stephensi shares habitats with An. arabiensis and An. amharicus. Larval presence was significantly associated with brick factory proximity (χ2 = 23.8, df = 5, p < 0.001), land use/surrounding environment (χ2 = 32.6, df = 13, p = 0.002), vegetation (χ2 = 27.1, df = 12, p = 0.008), shade coverage (χ2 = 25.9, df = 15, p = 0.039), substrate type (χ2 = 34.1, df = 6, p < 0.001), and competitor/predator presence (χ2 = 14.6, df = 1, p = 0.001). However, larval presence was not associated with the presence of larval interventions (χ2 = 1.3, df = 1, p = 0.250). Water pH (r = 0.26, n = 102, p < 0.050) and water pressure (r = 0.21, n = 102, p < 0.050) were the only water physicochemical parameters that were positively correlated with An. stephensi presence.
Anopheles stephensi was dominant in urban areas but was also present in rural areas. Existing larval source management methods do not prevent Anopheles from occurring in many habitats, indicating an urgent need for improved strategies.

articles.titulo: West Nile virus in Portugal: insights from equine serology.
articles.autores: Maroco D, Ramos F, Dos Santos FA, Henriques AM, Duarte A, Duarte M, Barros SC
articles.resumo_original:
West Nile virus (WNV) is a zoonotic mosquito-borne flavivirus belonging to the family Flaviviridae and the genus Orthoflavivirus. It is primarily transmitted by Culex spp. mosquitoes and maintained in an enzootic cycle involving avian hosts. Humans and horses are considered incidental or dead-end hosts, as they do not sustain onward transmission due to their low viremia levels, although infections may progress to severe neurological disease and death. In Portugal, WNV has circulated in horses almost annually since its first detection in 2004, suggesting endemic establishment.
This study provides updated data on the geographical distribution and annual occurrence of WNV infection in clinically affected horses in mainland Portugal between 2022 and 2025, thereby contributing to a broader understanding of WNV dynamics in southern Europe. As viremia is typically low and short-lived in horses, diagnosis relies primarily on serological methods, particularly the detection of IgM antibodies. IgM analyses identified WNV-seropositive horses in all four years, with 3/9 cases (33.3%) testing positive in 2022, 15/30 (50.0%) in 2023, 32/52 (61.5%) in 2024, and 13/38 (34.2%) in 2025. No WNV RNA was detected in serum samples. Based on clinical signs together with serological results, WNV was diagnosed in 63 of the 129 horses presenting neurological signs.
These findings reinforce the continued circulation of WNV in Portugal and highlight the importance of sustained surveillance in equine populations.

articles.titulo: Global stability analysis of within-host Zika virus-chikungunya virus co-infection with CTL immune responses.
articles.autores: Elaiw AM, Alkhudhari ZY, Almohaimeed EA, Hobiny AD
articles.resumo_original: We formulate and analyse a mathematical model for the within-host co-infection dynamics of Zika virus (ZIKV) and chikungunya virus (CHIKV), incorporating latently infected cells and cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) immune responses. We establish the nonnegativity and boundedness of solutions. Using the next-generation matrix method, we derive the basic reproduction numbers (RZL) and (RCL) for the ZIKV and CHIKV submodels, respectively, and the overall reproduction number (R0L=max{RZL,RCL}). Invasion reproduction numbers, (RZL,inv) and (RCL,inv), are derived to characterise the ability of either virus to invade an established infection. Global stability of the equilibria is established using Lyapunov functions. We investigate three therapeutic protocols: antiviral treatment blocking viral entry, treatment reducing viral production, and IL-2 therapy enhancing CTL responses. Sensitivity analysis of (RZL) and (RCL) is performed, and numerical simulations support the stability results. Simulations indicate that combined antiviral and immune-based interventions suppress co-infection by reducing viral replication and enhancing immune-mediated clearance.

articles.titulo: Novel dengue serotype 4 live virus human challenge: a phase 1 dose optimisation and homologous rechallenge study.
articles.autores: Chua JV, Price A, Sharaf S, Camacho Ortega S, Bernal PJ, Butler L, Koudjra AR, Joshi S, Hardy CSC, Currier JR, Waickman AT, Cairo C, Friberg H, Edelman R, Lyke KE
articles.resumo_original:
Dengue live virus human challenges (LVHCs) are key in dengue vaccine and pharmacological development, to down-select candidates and provide a useful platform for understanding viral-host immunology in a controlled setting. The primary aim of this study was to assess the safety, reactogenicity, and immunogenicity of a newly derived underattenuated dengue virus serotype-4-LVHC (DENV-4-LVHC) strain intended for future dengue challenge studies.
We conducted a first-in-human, phase 1, non-randomised, open-label study that evaluated the safety and optimised dose of the DENV-4-LVHC strain H-241 in flavivirus-naive healthy adult volunteers. The trial was conducted between April 28, 2022, and Dec 18, 2023, at the University of Maryland (Baltimore, MD, USA) and included a dose-optimisation study in which participants were enrolled into staggered-start, dose-ranging cohorts, beginning with the lowest dose, and homologous rechallenge substudy in which willing, primary-infected participants were rechallenged with the optimised dose of DENV-4 at least 12 months from the primary challenge. Successful challenge was defined as more than 90% participants developing self-limiting mild-to-moderate dengue symptoms with detectable RNAemia. Participants were analysed on the basis of the treatment group (primary infection vs rechallenge). This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT05268302).
14 healthy adult participants were enrolled between March 31, 2022, and June 9, 2022 (dose optimisation), and were challenged with a subcutaneous dose of DENV-4-LVHC on June 12, 2023 (rechallenge). The majority were men (11 [79%] of 14), and almost half were non-White (6 [43%]). The mean participant age was 33·6 years (range 20-48). All 14 participants developed viraemia and symptoms consistent with self-limited, mild-to-moderate dengue at an optimised dose of 95 plaque-forming units (low dose). Six (60%) participants (of the original ten from the 2022 cohort) were rechallenged using the optimised dose 1 year after primary challenge, and none developed detectable dengue. Robust antibody responses, plasmablast expansion, and antiviral gene upregulation were seen during primary infection but not after rechallenge. No severe dengue, need for inpatient observation, or dengue challenge-related serious adverse events were observed.
DENV-4-LVHC was found to be safe and highly predictable for use in future challenge studies, to evaluate vaccine and therapeutic candidates. Immunity from previous DENV-4-LVHC infection conferred protection following homologous rechallenge 1 year after primary exposure.

articles.titulo: Metabolite Screening Identifies Potent Antivirals that Mitigate Zika Virus-Induced Ocular Pathology.
articles.autores: Singh S, Jeyachandran AV, Daskou M, Zaiss A, Kolge H, Wright RE, Singhal A, Bonazzi A, Damoiseaux R, Arumugaswami V, Kumar A
articles.resumo_original: Zika virus (ZIKV) infection remains a significant global health threat due to its association with severe congenital, neurological, and ocular complications and the continued lack of approved antiviral therapies or vaccines. To identify new therapeutic candidates, we performed a high-throughput antiviral screen of 1,050 human endogenous and exosome-derived metabolites for their ability to attenuate ZIKV infection in human retinal pigment epithelial cells (RPE). This led to the identification of 10 metabolites that reduced ZIKV-induced cytopathic effects, which were further evaluated for antiviral activity and toxicity using physiologically relevant ocular infection models. Among these candidates, octanedioic acid, undecanedioic acid, and 10-undecen-1-ol emerged as the most effective, significantly reducing ZIKV replication and modulating innate immune responses in RPE cells. Analysis of host signaling revealed metabolite-associated changes in STAT1, AMPK, and YAP phosphorylation, identifying potential pathways tied to their antiviral activity. Importantly, in an immunocompetent mouse model of ZIKV-induced chorioretinal atrophy, treatment with these metabolites markedly reduced retinal lesions and immune cell infiltration, demonstrating in vivo therapeutic efficacy. Collectively, these findings identify host-derived metabolites as promising antiviral candidates against ZIKV and warrant further translational investigation.

articles.titulo: Dengue virus controlled human challenge reveals that preexisting immunity shapes viral replication and broadly protective responses.
articles.autores: Odio CD, Aogo RA, Firdous S, Voirin C, Blanco-Rivera S, Lowman KE, Asante N, Broderson Y, Konda K, Hasund CM, Martinez-Perez A, Mpingabo PI, Law M, Jarvis C, Callier V, Hunsberger S, Abad Fernandez M, de Silva A, Kattappuram R, Bhushan G, Yek C, Manning J, Durbin AP, Cohen JI, Weiskopf D, Whitehead SS, Katzelnick LC
articles.resumo_original: Dengue is the canonical viral disease for which immune history is a determinant of protective versus pathogenic responses and immunogenicity. Yet, because of limitations in animal models and clinical presentation after peak viremia, how preinfection and early immune responses affect dengue outcome is not confirmed. We conducted a phase 1 clinical trial with 45 healthy adults to test whether secondary infection challenge with a heterotypic, full-length, attenuated virus increases viremia and immunogenicity compared with primary and tertiary infection. Viremia was associated with more, but still mild, clinical signs and symptoms, and secondary infection resulted in greater viremia, neutralizing antibodies, and protective T cell responses. However, those whose baseline antibodies most efficiently increased dengue virus replication in an in vitro assay experienced delayed inflammatory and adaptive immune activation, the highest viremia, strong acute immune responses, and waning of potent CD8+ T cells and antibodies. In contrast, higher baseline antibodies against the nonstructural protein 1 of multiple serotypes predicted early interferon and balanced immune activation, viremia control, and development of enduring, potent B and T cells, revealing how vaccines can induce broad, long-lasting protection. Last, individuals with potent and neutralizing antibodies and IFN-γ+ T cells at baseline experienced minimal viral replication. Together, these findings demonstrate that controlled human challenge with dengue virus can delineate coordinated versus dysregulated acute immune responses and their effects on immunogenicity, informing therapeutic and vaccine strategies for dengue and other viral diseases.

articles.titulo: A Live Attenuated Dengue Virus Vaccine (Dengvaxia) is Suppressed in Individuals with Immunity to Serotype 4.
articles.autores: Adams C, Hein LD, White LJ, Shah R, Premkumar L, Daag JV, Agrupis KA, Crisostomo MV, Ylade M, Deen J, Lopez AL, de Silva AM
articles.resumo_original:
Dengvaxia® was the first live attenuated tetravalent dengue virus (DENV) vaccine to be tested and approved for use in people. While Dengvaxia was designed to be tetravalent, in humans, the vaccine performed like a monovalent DENV4 vaccine because the DENV4 vaccine virus replicated better than other vaccine serotypes. Dengvaxia® was safe and efficacious in children who were DENV-immune at baseline and contraindicated for use in DENV-naïve children.
When Dengvaxia® was rolled out as a pediatric vaccine in the Philippines in 2016, we established a prospective cohort to assess vaccine performance by baseline dengue serostatus. Here we report on how baseline monotypic immunity to each serotype (reflecting one past DENV infection) impacted Dengvaxia® responses.
We observed that in children with baseline immunity to DENV1, 2 or 3, the vaccine stimulated a secondary serotype cross-neutralizing Ab response, which likely explains the overall favorable performance of the vaccine in seropositive children enrolled in phase 3 trials. We observed a high frequency (61%) of vaccine suppression among DENV4 monotypic immune children.
Our results confirm the replication dominance of the DENV4 vaccine component in Dengvaxia® and directly implicate pre-existing DENV4 immunity in the suppression of the vaccine. Our results have broader implications for evaluating the performance of other DENV vaccines in seropositive individuals.

articles.titulo: mRNA-1273 SARS-CoV-2 vaccination in people with HIV: an immune correlates analysis of CD4 + T cell responses in the multicenter CoVPN 3008 observational study.
