articles.autores: Khuzwayo S, Zhang B, Voillet V, Carpp LN, LaherOmar F, Peng J, Hu J, Schwedhelm K, Smit E, Magaret CA, Chen Z, Heng S, Jin Y, Elyanu PJ, Tapley A, Kee JJ, Hudson A, Bhebhe S, Kaldine H, Kgagudi P, Hermanus T, Andriesen J, Randhawa AK, Fisher LH, Villaran M, Polakowski L, Yacovone M, Samandari T, Chirenje Z, Badal-Faesen S, Brumskine W, Coetzer S, Dawson R, Delany-Moretlwe S, Diacon AH, Fry S, Gill KM, Hoosain ZAE, Hosseinipour MC, Inambao M, Innes C, Innes S, Kalonji D, Kasaro M, Kassim P, Kayange N, Kamuti E, Kilembe W, Laher F, Makhema J, Malahleha M, Maluleke VL, Mathebula M, Mboya G, McHarry K, Kityo Mutuluuza C, Mda P, Mitha E, Msomi S, Moloantoa T, Naicker N, Naicker V, Nanvubya A, Nuwagaba-Biribonwoha H, Otieno W, Potgieter EL, Potloane D, Punt Z, Said JA, Singh Y, Tayob MS, Vahed Y, Maena J, Cohen MS, Kublin JG, Gail Bekker L, Corey L, Gray GE, Huang Y, Mgodi NM, Dadabhai S, Kotze PL, Garrett N, Hural J, Ferrari G, Montefiori D, Moore PL, Tomaras GD, Mkhize NN, De Rosa SC, McElrath MJ, Gilbert PB, Andersen-Nissen E
articles.resumo_original: T cell correlates of COVID-19 risk are poorly defined, particularly in people with HIV (PWH). CoVPN 3008 ( NCT05168813 ) Part A was a prospective 14,002-participant cohort study that administered one or two doses of mRNA-1273 COVID-19 vaccine, depending on baseline SARS-CoV-2 serostatus, in participants (83% PWH) in sub-Saharan Africa. Participants self-monitored for prespecified COVID-19 symptoms, defined by Centers for Disease Control and Prevention symptom criteria. Previous work showed that protection from COVID-19 was superior for hybrid versus vaccine-induced immunity, and that neutralizing antibody titers inversely associated with COVID-19 risk. In the present work, we measured T cell responses to Spike and Nucleocapsid at baseline and 4 weeks post last-vaccination (Peak) in a case-cohort study and assessed them as correlates of risk. In Hybrid Group PWH (n = 22 cases), COVID-19 risk over 6 months decreased with increasing Peak Spike BA.4/5-specific CD4 + T cell responses, from 15.8%, 4.7%, and 0% risk at 0.1%, 0.2%, and 0.3% IFN-γ and/or IL-2 response magnitude, respectively. Including baseline Spike-specific neutralizing antibody titer and Peak CD4 + T cell functionality score in the same model increased the association's strength (overall p < 0.001). Thus, CD4 + T cell responses are an independent correlate of COVID-19 risk among PWH with pre-existing SARS-CoV-2 immunity.

articles.titulo: Potent reaction hijacking inhibitors of Plasmodium falciparum asparagine tRNA synthetase.
articles.autores: Ye X, Esherick LY, Ketprasit N, Narwal SK, Godoy LC, Boonyalai N, Dogovski C, Morton CJ, Rabie T, Famodimu MT, Tai C-W, Yeo T, Donnelly O, Orta LV, Anderson I, Jeon JH, Le LHM, Leeming MG, Laureano De Souza M, Chenu E, Creek DJ, Delves MJ, Birkholtz L-M, Duffy J, Lobb K, Durst G, Lee MCS, Fidock DA, Niles JC, Siegel MG, Tilley L, Xie SC
articles.resumo_original:
Malaria remains one of the major threats to human health. Breakthrough drugs with high potency and low resistance risk are needed to combat the ever-increasing resistance to currently deployed antimalarials. Here, we explore a series of 4-aminoquinazoline-based sulfonamides (4AQS), with a synthetically accessible scaffold. Exemplars exhibit nanomolar potency against blood stage Plasmodium cultures, with up to 300-fold selectivity compared with a mammalian cell line. The compounds are active against transmissible stages of Plasmodium falciparum and refractory to resistance development. Targeted mass spectrometry reveals that the 4AQS compounds act as reaction hijacking inhibitors targeting P. falciparum aminoacyl tRNA synthetases (aaRSs). Subtle changes to the chemical structure switch the main target from cytoplasmic threonine tRNA synthetase (PfThrRS) to cytoplasmic asparagine tRNA synthetase (PfAsnRS), a change that is associated with increased potency against P. falciparum. The target preference was confirmed by selective knockdown of different P. falciparum aaRSs and by tolerance selection in a mutator line. Consistent with aaRS targets, exemplar compounds activate the amino acid starvation response. Recombinant enzyme inhibition and thermal stabilization assays confirm the susceptibility of PfAsnRS to reaction hijacking and show that human AsnRS is less susceptible. A molecular model of Asn-tRNA-bound PfAsnRS reveals that a potent hijacker adopts a pose similar to adenosine 5'-monophosphate (AMP). An AlphaFold model of the native PfAsnRS dimer helps explain the tolerance-conferring effect of a mutation at the dimer interface.
Every year, at least 200 million new malaria infections are diagnosed, causing more than 600,000 deaths in Africa and Southeast Asia. Ever-increasing levels of resistance to current antimalarials are leading to an impending crisis. Breakthrough drugs with new modes of action are much needed. Here, we explore a series of inhibitors that hijack critical malaria parasite enzymes. The target enzymes catalyze the formation of a bond between the hijackers and an enzyme substrate, forming a tight-binding compound that disrupts the malaria parasite's protein translation machinery. The hijacking inhibitors exhibit high-level potency against the disease-causing stage of the malaria parasite and are also active against transmissible stages. They exhibit up to 300-fold selectivity compared with a mammalian cell line, possess drug-like chemical attributes, and are easily synthesized. Importantly, the compounds are refractory to resistance development.

articles.titulo: Clinical Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax Infections in the Ethiopian Highlands Were Uncommonly Associated with Recent Travel.
articles.revista: The American journal of tropical medicine and hygiene
articles.autores: Lown LA, Ewnetu Y, Carlier L, Lemma W, Berhane N, Koepfli C
articles.resumo_original: The Ethiopian highlands were historically believed to be malaria-free, yet clinical cases are frequently observed in health centers at elevations above 2,000 m. The proportion of cases that recently returned from the lowlands where malaria is endemic, seasonal patterns, and risk factors for infection are poorly described. Febrile patients were enrolled from November 2019 to September 2020 in a health center in Gondar, Ethiopia, at an elevation of 2,100 m. Plasmodium falciparum and P. vivax were detected by microscopy conducted at the health center and by quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR). A total of 183 P. falciparum infections were typed for hrp2 and hrp3 gene deletions (hrp2: 2.7%; hrp3: 55.2%; dual: 21.9%), and 1,819 participants were enrolled. Test positivity by microscopy and qPCR was 58.1% and 64.1% for P. falciparum, and 41.8% and 35.9% for P. vivax; 3.1% of individuals reported travel to the lowlands within 4 weeks prior to sample collection. Travel increased the odds of malaria infection by 4.1 times, but 92.4% of individuals who tested positive did not report travel. Adults 16 to 35 years of age accounted for 57% of individuals who presented for testing, and test positivity peaked in this age group (P. falciparum: 27.3%; P. vivax: 10.9%). Most individuals who were malaria-positive had not traveled, suggesting that local transmission is occurring within the Ethiopian highlands. The concentration of infections in adult males points to a strong behavior-related risk of infection.

articles.titulo: From Asia to Africa: drivers of antimalarial drug resistance emergence and spread.
articles.autores: Serrato-Arroyo S, Segovia X, Huijben S
articles.resumo_original: Antimalarial drug resistance has repeatedly become established first in Southeast Asia and subsequently spread to sub-Saharan Africa, despite Africa bearing most of the global malaria burden. We evaluate eight hypotheses proposed to explain this pattern, spanning transmission intensity, parasite, host and vector biology, and treatment practices. We distinguish between the generation, establishment, expansion, and geographic spread of resistance, as these stages may be affected differently. The strongest evidence supports roles for transmission-dependent processes and earlier and more intense historical drug pressure. Parasite genetic background may also be important, while evidence for human genetics, recombination, vector-mediated effects, and poor-quality drugs is weaker. Overall, resistance emergence is likely shaped by multiple interacting pressures acting across parasite, vector, host, and health system scales.

articles.titulo: Dehydration in Tropical Fevers: Rethinking Fluid and Electrolyte Replacement.
articles.autores: Chatterjee N, Gilada T, Patil A, Malve H, Chamle V, Bangale N
articles.resumo_original: Tropical fevers, including dengue, malaria, typhoid, chikungunya, leptospirosis, and scrub typhus, impose a substantial and growing public health burden in the tropical and subtropical regions, particularly the Indian subcontinent. Climate change, monsoon season, and inadequate sanitation further exacerbate transmission dynamics and outbreak patterns. Dehydration represents a critical yet frequently underrecognized complication of these infections. It is attributed to high-grade fever, vomiting, excessive sweating, decreased oral intake, and pathophysiological mechanisms, such as plasma leakage in dengue, hemolysis in malaria, and gastrointestinal losses in typhoid. Electrolyte disturbances, specifically hyponatremia, hypokalemia, and hypochloremia, contribute to the severity of these conditions and likelihood of multi-organ failure. Inadequate hydration amplifies underlying physiological dysfunction, including hemoconcentration, hypovolemic shock, acute kidney injury, and cardiovascular compromise, thereby increasing hospitalization rates, morbidity, and mortality. This review explores the disease-specific hydration challenges across diverse tropical fevers and evaluates the current strategies for effective fluid management. The World Health Organization (WHO), United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund (UNICEF), and national guidelines recommend oral rehydration therapy, formulated with optimized sodium and glucose concentrations to promote rehydration through facilitation of the intestinal sodium-glucose co-transporter (SGLT1) mechanism for management of ambulatory and mild-to-moderate cases. Its efficacy in symptom relief, minimizing intravenous fluid requirements, and accelerating clinical recovery is well established. However, individualized and careful calibration of fluid management remains essential to prevent fluid overload and other related complications. Thus, integrating standardized, evidence-based hydration protocols into routine clinical practice holds the potential to be a practical and cost-effective strategy for managing tropical infection in India and other regions with similar climatic and epidemiological settings.

articles.titulo: High prevalence of pfmdr1 and pfpm2 amplification and pfmdr1 haplotypes in Plasmodium falciparum isolates circulating in Ghana.
articles.autores: Kassim AR, Younge PA, Dorvi IN, Saiid S, Sakyi ME, Ahmed O, Kudakpo AY, Addo ST, Yeboah SN, Mensah C, Debrah I, Morang'a CM, Amuzu DSY, Awandare GA, Aniweh Y, Amenga-Etego LN
articles.resumo_original:
In Ghana, artemether-lumefantrine (AL), and artesunate-amodiaquine (AS-AQ) are the main first-line ACTs for uncomplicated malaria, with dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DHA-PPQ) as an alternative treatment regimen. Copy Number Polymorphisms (CNPs) in Plasmodium falciparum multidrug resistance 1 (pfmdr1) and plasmepsin 2 (pfpm2) genes, as well as specific pfmdr1 haplotypes have been implicated in resistance to AL and DHA-PPQ partner drugs.
This study characterised pfmdr1 and pfpm2 CNPs and pfmdr1 haplotypes in 900 clinical malaria samples across three transmission zones in Ghana. Using a SYBR Green-based Quantitative real-time Polymerase Chain Reaction (qPCR) assay, followed by targeted amplicon sequencing.
Successful pfmdr1 and pfpm2 amplifications were detected in 32.0% (n = 288) and 27.8% (n = 250) isolates respectively. No significant difference in the prevalence of these gene amplifications was observed across the three eco-epidemiological zones (pfmdr1: p = 0.888; pfpm2: p = 0.081). Furthermore, a weak positive correlation was observed between pfmdr1 and pfpm2 copy numbers (ρ = 0.196), suggesting limited co-selection of these loci. Pfmdr1 haplotype analysis at codons N86Y, Y184F, and D1246Y revealed a high prevalence (55.6%) of the NFD haplotype linked to lumefantrine selection. Interestingly, this haplotype allele was equally prevalent among isolates carrying single or multiple gene copy numbers.
Taken together, this study observed increased prevalence of pfmdr1 and pfpm2 gene amplification in Ghana. Also, a high frequency of the single mutant NFD pfmdr1 haplotype suggesting ongoing selection pressure potentially driven by widespread AL use in Ghana. In addition, pfpm2 CNP has been associated with piperaquine resistance. These findings provide a critical baseline for ongoing molecular surveillance as an early warning for ACT partner drug resistance in Ghana.

articles.titulo: First report of culturable fungi associated with the Brazilian sharpnose shark (Rhizoprionodon lalandii) from southeastern Brazil.
articles.autores: Oliveira MME, da Costa GL, de Souza BA, de Oliveira Baptista B, Barbosa BF, Hauser-Davis RA
articles.resumo_original:
Climate change and other anthropogenic environmental changes may alter fungal distributions and ecological interactions, potentially facilitating the emergence or redistribution of opportunistic fungi in marine ecosystems. These shifts raise concerns regarding microbial contamination in seafood and the need for surveillance in marine organisms. Elasmobranchs, such as sharks and rays, are ecologically and economically important but remain understudied regarding fungal occurrence in wild populations. This study provides the first report of cultivable fungal taxa associated with the Brazilian sharpnose shark (Rhizoprionodon lalandii) from southeastern Brazil.
Swabs from the mouth, gills, and cloaca were obtained from 22 specimens procured from artisanal fisheries in Cabo Frio, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Fungal occurrence varied among sampled anatomical sites and individuals, with several cloacal samples showing abundant growth under the culture conditions employed. Recovered isolates consisted primarily of members of the Candida parapsilosis species complex and Meyerozyma guilliermondii, alongside occasional detection of other yeast taxa including Rhodotorula mucilaginosa, Debaryomyces hansenii, Trichosporon japonicum, and Pichia terricola. Because fungal recovery relied on culture-based methods, ITS sequencing of representative colonies, and sampling restricted to external and cloacal tissues, the detected assemblage likely reflects predominant culturable taxa rather than total fungal diversity. Furthermore, implications for food safety, transmission pathways, or environmental contamination remain speculative and warrant targeted investigation.
These findings expand current knowledge regarding fungi associated with R. lalandii and highlight the need for additional studies incorporating environmental sampling, edible tissue analyses, and broader fungal characterization approaches to better understand potential ecological and public health implications.

articles.titulo: Mechanisms and therapeutic perspectives of mucosal glycosylation-innate immunity crosstalk in inflammatory bowel disease (Review).
articles.autores: Liu X, Zhang T, Jin J, Song Y, Li M, Zhong H, Cai M, Ding S, Han X
articles.resumo_original: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a group of chronic, relapsing inflammatory disorders of the gastrointestinal tract, driven by a complex interplay of genetic susceptibility, environmental exposures, intestinal microbiota dysbiosis and immune dysregulation. In recent years, mucosal glycosylation has emerged as a fundamental molecular determinant of intestinal barrier integrity and function and is increasingly recognized as a key regulatory interface linking the microbiota with host immune responses. Concurrently, the innate immune system serves an important role in mucosal defense and inflammatory responses through pattern recognition receptor‑mediated signaling, and its aberrant activation represents a key driver of persistent inflammation in IBD. The present review systematically summarizes the bidirectional regulatory crosstalk between mucosal glycosylation and innate immunity. The mechanistic roles of glycosylation modifications are highlighted in pathogen recognition, inflammatory signal transduction, inflammasome activation and maintenance of mucosal barrier integrity. Conversely, it is discussed how innate immune activation regulates glycan biosynthesis and remodeling through inflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress and major signaling pathways, thereby reshaping the mucosal glycome in disease contexts. On this basis, the dynamic alterations of glycosylation‑innate immunity interactions across different stages of IBD, including disease initiation, progression and relapse, are delineated, emphasizing their important role in sustaining chronic inflammation and driving tissue remodeling. In addition, emerging therapeutic strategies targeting glycosylation pathways, glycan‑lectin interactions, mucosal barrier restoration and microbiota modulation are summarized. The potential of glycomics, multi‑omics integration and glyco‑immune biomarkers in disease stratification and precision medicine are also discussed. By integrating perspectives from glycobiology and immunology, the present review aims to provide a conceptual framework and novel directions for mechanistic research and targeted therapy in IBD.

articles.titulo: Spatiotemporally coordinated immunometabolic-hyperthermia therapy for diabetic bone defect regeneration.
articles.autores: Wang L, Peng X, Zheng L, Liu Y, Chen L, Li X, Wang Z
articles.resumo_original: Diabetic bone defects (DBDs) are typified by persistent inflammation, oxidative stress, and microbial infection within the diabetic microenvironment, which collectively hinder osteogenesis and angiogenesis. Herein, we introduce an Immunometabolic-Hyperthermia Therapy (IMHT) strategy based on a dual-functional nanoplatform, namely a polydopamine/itaconate-incorporated agarose/gelatin (PIAG) hydrogel. This system is fabricated by incorporating itaconic acid (ITA) into polydopamine (PDA) nanoparticles through in situ polymerization, followed by encapsulation within a gelatin/agarose matrix. ITA primarily provides immunometabolic regulation, while PDA enables a tunable photothermal response. Upon localized photothermal heating (∼50 °C), the PIAG hydrogel effectively disrupts bacterial biofilms, with photothermal treatment providing the dominant antibacterial effect and ITA offering an additional supportive contribution. Upon mild photothermal activation (∼41 °C), IMHT mitigates excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, inhibits neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, and reprograms macrophages toward an M2-like reparative phenotype through JAK1/STAT1 pathway inhibition. The resulting pro-regenerative immune milieu enhances fibroblast growth factor-2 (FGF-2) secretion, while heat-induced activation of HSP90 stabilizes FGF-2/FGFR1 signaling, further promoting osteogenic differentiation and endothelial migration. Overall, the spatiotemporally coordinated antibacterial, immunometabolic, and regenerative regulation realized by IMHT offers a comprehensive and effective strategy for the repair of diabetic bone defects.

articles.titulo: From expression profiling to functional validation: evidence hierarchy and biomarker readiness of circular RNAs in aquatic animals.
articles.autores: Song KS, Guo M, Li CH
articles.resumo_original: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are covalently closed non-coding RNA molecules that are mainly generated from precursor mRNAs through back-splicing. Owing to the lack of free 5' and 3' ends, circRNAs exhibit high stability and pronounced spatiotemporal expression specificity. In aquatic animals, recent advances in high-throughput sequencing and bioinformatic analysis have greatly expanded the catalog of circRNAs and uncovered their regulatory roles in growth, gonadal development, tissue regeneration, immune defense, and environmental stress responses. This review provides a systematic overview of circRNA biogenesis, representative molecular functions, identification strategies, and bioinformatic resources in aquatic animals, with particular emphasis on circRNA-mediated regulation during bacterial and viral infection, antiparasitic defense, trained immunity, and responses to physicochemical stressors. We further summarize the current evidence supporting the potential of circRNAs as candidate biomarkers for economically important traits, infectious disease monitoring, and ecotoxicological assessment. Importantly, we highlight the major bottlenecks that currently limit progress in this field, including incomplete genome annotation, algorithm-dependent identification bias, and the lack of robust in vivo functional validation. Overall, aquatic animals provide valuable non-model systems for expanding our understanding of circRNA biology, although many proposed regulatory mechanisms and translational applications remain to be further validated.

articles.titulo: Atherosclerosis: From Pathogenesis to Therapeutic Interventions.
articles.autores: Zhou E, Zhan C, Li Y, Zeng Y, Luo R, Ouyang X, Liu S, Yang R, Yan N, Jiang L
articles.resumo_original: Atherosclerosis is no longer viewed solely as a lipid-storage disorder but rather as a complex multisystem inflammatory disease driven by interactions among the vascular, immune, metabolic, and nervous systems. This review integrates recent concepts, including trained immunity, the neuroimmune cardiovascular interface, vascular cell plasticity, and the microbiome-vascular axis, that reshape the understanding of plaque initiation, progression, and instability. We summarize how established lipid-lowering, antidiabetic, antihypertensive, and revascularization strategies influence atherosclerotic disease and discuss emerging interventions, including RNA therapeutics, anti-inflammatory agents, gene therapy, and cell-based approaches. Key ongoing clinical trials that may clarify the cardiovascular benefits and safety of these strategies are also reviewed. Despite therapeutic advances, residual cardiovascular risk persists because of limitations in animal models, sex-related differences in plaque phenotype, and the lack of clinically applicable biomarkers. Nanotechnology, human microphysiological systems, spatial multiomics, and artificial intelligence may help bridge these translational gaps. Successful clinical implementation will nevertheless require biomarker-guided patient selection, rational combination therapy, validated surrogate endpoints, long-term safety assessment, and attention to health economics. In summary, these advances will shape future translational research and clinical trial design, ultimately advancing personalized management of atherosclerosis.

articles.titulo: Ginsenoside Rd alleviates atherosclerosis by inhibiting adipocyte ferroptosis in perivascular adipose tissues.
articles.autores: Fu X, Liu C, Hu F, Qin J, Wang T, Li X
articles.resumo_original:
Ginsenoside Rd (Rd) is an active ingredient in Panax ginseng Meyer and can be absorbed into the adipose tissue. Here, we aimed to investigate the impact of Rd on atherosclerosis (AS) and explore the mechanism.
We constructed an AS model by feeding ApoE-/- mice with a standard Western high-fat diet, treated with Rd, and combined RORC and TIGAR adipocyte-specific adeno-associated virus infection. An inflammatory adipocyte model (3T3-L1) was induced by LPS, and a lipid accumulation model in adipocytes was induced by palmitic acid. We investigated the role of the Rd-mediated RORC/TIGAR axis in adipocyte inflammation, oxidative stress, and ferroptosis through lentiviral vectors and the ferroptosis activator erastin. The interactions between RORC and TIGAR were examined. Next, the degree of lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis within perivascular adipose tissues (PVAT) in mice and 3T3-L1 cells was assessed.
Rd improved PVAT dysfunction and alleviated endothelial inflammation in AS mice. Rd targeted and inhibited RORC expression in adipocytes within the PVAT of mice. The transcription factor RORC occupied the TIGAR promoter to repress TIGAR transcription. Reactivation of RORC reversed the therapeutic benefit of Rd on AS, and reactivation of TIGAR also alleviated AS exacerbated by RORC. Rd reached therapeutic benefits by inhibiting RORC expression in adipocytes within PVAT, weakening its inhibitory effect on TIGAR, and further inhibiting adipocyte ferroptosis.
Rd targets RORC to activate TIGAR expression and block adipocyte ferroptosis in PVAT, thereby inhibiting AS.

articles.titulo: Metabolic licensing of innate immune memory.
articles.autores: Mhlanga MM, Pieper AA
articles.resumo_original: NAD+ is revealed to be a metabolic signal that preserves an epigenetic mark central to trained immunity by inhibiting the histone demethylase KDM5a (see related Research Article by Jin et al.).

articles.titulo: Nuclear NAD+ promotes innate immune memory by inhibiting KDM5A-dependent histone demethylation.
articles.autores: Jin H, Wang Z, Liu Y, Wang Z, Li M, Xue J, Zhang Y, Yu T, Wang S, Huo B, Li C, Wang X, Yao R, Zhang H, Yi J, Lin Y, Cui L, Guo H, Guo Z, Zhang L, Pan C, Shen X, Wang G, Fan G, Wu Z, Tan J, Gao S, Bei JX, Huang P, Liu J, Xia X
articles.resumo_original: Trained immunity is tightly regulated by metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming, yet how these changes are orchestrated at the chromatin level to establish long-term innate immune memory is not fully understood. Here, we show that induction of trained immunity elevates nuclear levels of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), which directly binds to KDM5A demethylase and inhibits its activity, thereby sustaining H3K4me3 (histone H3 lysine 4 trimethylation) levels and chromatin accessibility at inflammatory gene promoters to enhance "memory" responsiveness upon restimulation. Genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT), the rate-limiting enzyme for NAD+ synthesis, impaired trained immunity and associated antitumor activity. Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) supplementation rescued defective trained immunity-mediated antitumor activity in NAMPT-deficient and aged mice. In human cancer, NAMPT expression in myeloid cells correlated with an inflammatory tumor microenvironment. Our findings identify KDM5A as a nuclear NAD+ sensor that orchestrates histone methylation and chromatin accessibility required for trained immunity.

articles.titulo: Lipid-sensing GPR183-KRAS signaling mediates TH17 autoimmunity and identifies fluvoxamine repurposing in uveitis.
articles.autores: Zhang C, Liu X, Xu N, Chen H, Gao Y, Gu C, Shen X, Wu J, Lu X, Zhang P, He Y, Xu Z, Su W
articles.resumo_original: Autoimmune uveitis (AU) is a leading cause of irreversible blindness driven by pathogenic T helper 17 (TH17) cell-mediated inflammation, yet current therapies are limited by efficacy and side effects, with immunometabolic mechanisms remaining poorly defined. By integrating single-cell RNA sequencing and multilayered metabolomic profiling in patients with AU and experimental AU models, we identified the lipid-sensing G protein-coupled receptor GPR183 as a key immunometabolic regulator in pathogenic CD4+ T cells. Upon activation, GPR183 modulates intracellular signaling via suppression of cyclic adenosine monophosphate-cAMP-dependent protein kinase activity and promotion of son-of-sevenless-dependent KRAS activation, which in turn elicits copper overload-induced mitochondrial oxidative stress, structural impairment, and metabolic rewiring toward glycolysis, thereby promoting TH17 cell pathogenicity. For clinical translation, virtual screening of Food and Drug Administration-approved drugs coupled with molecular docking and microscale thermophoresis validation identified fluvoxamine (FLV) as a direct GPR183 antagonist. In in vivo and in vitro uveitis and colitis models, FLV attenuated GPR183-KRAS signaling, dampened pathogenic TH17 cell responses, and alleviated tissue inflammation. These findings delineate a unique GPR183-KRAS-mitochondrial damage axis governing TH17-driven autoimmunity and support repurposing FLV as a translatable therapeutic approach for AU and other autoimmune inflammatory disorders.

articles.titulo: Synthetic auxotrophy reveals metabolic regulation of plasma cell generation, affinity maturation, and cytokine receptor signaling.
articles.autores: Cho SH, Brookens SK, Raybuck AL, Meyer K, Paik Y, Hamilton J, Li J, Kalecky K, Park C, Lim J, Hicks SL, Karijolich J, Bottiglieri TH, Rathmell JC, Mogilenko D, Scharer CD, Boothby MR
articles.resumo_original: The proliferation and development of activated B lymphocytes into antibody (Ab)-secreting plasma cells are critical determinants of humoral immunity and sustain certain autoimmune diseases. Specific pathways and substrate supplies in intermediary metabolism influence lymphocyte differentiation and function. We now show that although stringent restriction of glutamine supply decreases B cell proliferation and differentiation into plasma cells, glutaminolysis - a major metabolic use of this amino acid - was only conditionally crucial in B cells and the Ab responses derived from them. Gls, the gene encoding the main glutaminase of lymphocytes, promoted anti-NP Ab responses at the primary and recall phases if either glucose uptake into mouse B cells or pyruvate into their mitochondria was also impaired. Otherwise, it was dispensable. This synthetic auxotrophy, that is, the conditional requirement of glutaminase for processes in addition to survival, involved supporting progressive expansion of mitochondrial respiration followed by plasma cell differentiation. Surprisingly, impairment of glutaminase and the mitochondrial pyruvate channel decreased IL-21 stimulation of STAT3 phosphorylation as well as interferon stimulation of STAT1 activation. Together, our findings establish a powerful collaboration of metabolic pathways in programming increased respiration and the development of Ab-secreting cells, but also reveal modulation of cytokine receptor signaling by metabolism.

articles.titulo: Immunological signatures of sepsis in abdominal solid organ transplant recipients: A multilayer and multicentric prospective cohort study.
articles.autores: Witowski A, Bracht T, Kröger L, Rump K, Nowak H, Bergmann L, Unterberg M, Rahmel T, Westhus B, Wolf A, Thon P, Ziehe D, Putensen C, Ehrentraut S, Zarbock A, Wappler F, Defosse J, Henzler D, Sitek B, Schnitzbauer A, Stervbo U, Rosiewicz K, Hugo C, Neumann S, Pagel P, Pascher A, Babel N, Adamzik M, Dyck B, Koos B
articles.resumo_original:
Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction resulting from a dysregulated host response to infection. Patients with prior abdominal solid organ transplantation (SOT) are highly susceptible to infection due to chronic immunosuppression, yet exhibit improved survival once sepsis occurs. The underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood.
We conducted a post hoc analysis within a prospective multicenter cohort of septic patients (SepsisDataNet.NRW; n = 538). Clinical outcomes were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox regression. Immune profiling included serum cytokines, flow cytometric immunophenotyping, plasma proteomics, and intracellular signaling using proximity ligation assays (PLA) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). To reduce clinical confounding, complementary exploratory analyses were performed in a non-septic kidney transplant cohort (e:KID).
SOT patients demonstrated improved 30-day survival compared with non-SOT patients (84% vs. 66%; adjusted HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.26-0.95). Cytokine analysis revealed lower IL-6 and TNF-α levels alongside higher IL-18 concentrations, indicating an altered inflammatory profile. Flow cytometry showed reductions in adaptive immune cells but relatively preserved innate immune function, reflected by higher monocytic HLA-DR expression. Proteomics identified enrichment of innate immune, complement, and lipid metabolic response networks. PLA-based cellular analyses revealed increased GLUT1 expression and enhanced TFAM/TFB2M interaction in SOT patients, indicating a distinct immunometabolic marker profile. In e:KID patients paired serum metabolomics demonstrated higher glucose and lower lactate concentrations 12 months after transplantation, accompanied by broader alterations in lipid and branched-chain amino acid profiles.
In patients with sepsis, abdominal SOT is associated with significant better survival than in non-SOT patients. Septic abdominal SOT patients display a distinct immune phenotype characterized by attenuated systemic inflammation, relative preservation of selected innate immune readouts, and alterations in immunometabolic markers.

articles.titulo: Functional consequences of acanthocephalan infection in Homarus americanus and advances in understanding of parasite-associated changes in lobster immunity.
articles.autores: Ghiasvand Z, MacCormack TJ, Rampaul M, Pickett S, Clark KF
articles.resumo_original: Profilicollis botulus is an acanthocephalan parasite with larval stages developing in arthropod intermediate hosts and adult stages maturing in vertebrate definitive hosts, typically seabirds. Despite its widespread occurrence in coastal ecosystems, the physiological and molecular consequences of P. botulus infection in the American lobster (Homarus americanus) remain unclear. In this exploratory observational study, we combined whole-animal respirometry with hepatopancreas RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) to characterize physiological and transcriptional differences between naturally infected and uninfected lobsters. Infected lobsters exhibited significantly lower mass-specific oxygen consumption than uninfected individuals (28.51 ± 1.87 vs 35.02 ± 1.49 mg O₂ kg-1 h-1). Exploratory transcriptomic analysis of a limited number of individuals (four infected and three uninfected) identified 324 differentially expressed genes (FDR < 0.05), including 232 downregulated and 92 upregulated transcripts in infected lobsters. Several transcripts associated with glycolysis and related metabolic processes showed higher expression in infected individuals. Conversely, lower transcript abundance was observed for multiple genes associated with innate immune functions, including lectin-type pattern recognition receptors, antimicrobial peptides (including anti-lipopolysaccharide factors), and components of the prophenoloxidase and coagulation systems, antioxidant enzymes, acute-phase proteins, and crustacean hyperglycemic hormone. Together, these findings associate reduced aerobic metabolism with lower expression of multiple innate immune-related transcripts in the hepatopancreas, a pattern that may be compatible with a stabilized host-parasite interaction and altered energetic allocation during parasitism. However, given the observational design and limited transcriptomic sample size, these interpretations remain hypotheses rather than demonstrated mechanisms. Together with other studies of parasite infections in crustaceans, our findings suggest that host responses to acanthocephalan infection may be host-dependent and influenced by parasite biology, tissue specificity, and host physiological condition. Further studies incorporating larger sample sizes, controlled infection experiments, and functional measurements are needed to determine whether these associations reflect direct effects of infection or other host-related and environmental factors.

articles.titulo: NLRP3 inflammasome dysregulation in chronic bacterial infections: mechanistic insights into treatment failure and relapse.
articles.autores: Girdhar J, Jangra S, Rastogi A, Saxena R
articles.resumo_original: Chronic and recurrent bacterial infections are a significant clinical issue despite the development of antimicrobial treatment. It is increasingly being shown that chronic host-based inflammatory dysregulation is also an integral cause of treatment failure and persistence of illness, and not just the consequence of microbial resistance. The NLRP3 inflammasome presents an important integrated platform linking tissue destruction, metabolic strain, and microbial detection to augmented inflammatory reactions. The ultimate goal of the review is to assess chronic bacterial infection as an inflammatory resolution dysfunction, and the example of persistent NLRP3 inflammasome dysregulation and the therapeutic consequences. In this review, the existing data on the canonical and non-canonical pathways of NLRP3 activation is summarized and the interplay between metabolic reprogramming, ionic flux, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired autophagy are all thought to contribute to the lowered activation thresholds in chronic infection. The disease-specific pathology of the prolonged IL-1β and IL-18 generation, destabilisation of the barricade and inflammatory feedback prolongation are common pathological themes in contexts like granulomatous lung disease, intracellular persistence syndromes, biofilm-associated infections and chronic airway colonisation. Inflammasome permissiveness and resolution are exacerbated by immunometabolic changes and microbiome imbalance.

articles.titulo: Dietary Fiber Improves High-Fat Diet-Induced Hyperglycemia by Modulating Intestinal ILC3-Mediated Immunity through the SCFA-FFAR2 Pathway.
articles.revista: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
articles.autores: Mou Y, Long F, Qi C, Huang W, Du Q, Zhang Y, Yu C, Zhou J
articles.resumo_original: Dietary fiber intake is associated with improved glycemic control in high-fat diet-induced hyperglycemia, yet the immunological mechanisms linking gut microbiota-derived metabolites to host defense remain poorly defined. Here, we investigated whether dietary fiber ameliorates these metabolic disorders by modulating intestinal group 3 innate lymphoid cells (ILC3s) via short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and their receptor FFAR2. In a 12-week fiber-supplemented high-fat diet mouse model, fiber alleviated hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, and intestinal barrier dysfunction. Mechanistically, fiber increased cecal SCFAs (especially propionate), which activated colonic ILC3s in an FFAR2-dependent manner. FFAR2 triggered ERK and STAT3 phosphorylation and directly bound STAT3 to facilitate its phosphorylation, boosting IL-22 transcription. SCFA-activated ILC3s strengthened epithelial barrier integrity via elevated tight-junction proteins. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that dietary fiber restores gut barrier function through the SCFA-FFAR2-ERK/STAT3-IL-22 axis in ILC 3s, highlighting ILC3-expressed FFAR2 as a potential therapeutic target for high-fat diet-related metabolic disorders.

articles.titulo: Gut bacterial lauroyl tryptamine reduces GPR183-associated inflammatory responses in human macrophages and T cells in vitro.
articles.autores: Lezzerini M, Spek V, Fung ICN, Müller MJ, Kubelka A, Sieber S, de Jonge WJ, Li Yim AYF, Te Velde AA, Zhang J
articles.resumo_original:
Recent research has highlighted the role of gut microbiota in producing bioactive metabolites that interact with G-protein coupled receptors (GPRs) and influence immune responses. Lauroyl tryptamine (LT), a metabolite produced by Agathobacter rectalis (formerly Eubacterium rectale), has been reported to antagonize GPR183, a receptor implicated in inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD). LT inhibits the binding of GPR183 with its natural ligands 7a,25-dihydroxycholesterol (OHC).
Here, we analyzed the GPR183 gene expression in intestinal tissues from IBD patients and non-IBD controls, as well as our previous single-cell transcriptomic dataset to identify key GPR183-expressing cells. We then use in vitro THP-1 derived macrophage and Jurkat T cell culture to test the effects of LT on inflammatory responses.
The GPR183 gene expression is elevated specifically in colonic and rectal tissues of ulcerative colitis patients, but not in Crohn's disease or ileal tissue. By analyzing single-cell transcriptomic dataset, we identified monocytes/macrophages, T cells, B cells, and innate lymphoid cells as key GPR183-expressing populations in human intestine. Using cell culture models, we demonstrated that LT modulates inflammatory pathways. In LPS-stimulated macrophages, OHC increased transcription of pro-inflammatory genes IL6, TNFA, and IL1B, which are reduced by LT. In activated Jurkat T cells, LT slightly decreased the OHC-mediated increase in the transcription of IL2. These findings support the hypothesis that LT, a known GPR183 antagonist, could modulate GPR183-associated inflammation in human macrophages and T cells in a context- and cell type-dependent manner, offering potential mechanistic insights into bioactive metabolite-mediated host-microbiota interactions in human intestine.

articles.titulo: New strategies for the treatment of tuberculosis: research progress and clinical translation in immune modulation and inflammation control.
articles.autores: Du S, Zhen L, Zhou J, Deng D
articles.resumo_original: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global public health challenge, with treatment complicated by drug resistance, adverse effects, and suboptimal host immune responses. Whilst conventional anti-TB drugs are effective bactericidally, their immunomodulatory effects may, in certain contexts, contribute to immune imbalance and affect treatment outcomes. Host-directed therapy (HDT), which aims to modulate the host immune response to enhance pathogen control and limit immunopathology, has emerged as a promising adjunctive strategy. This narrative review critically evaluates the current evidence for HDT in TB, focusing on immunosenescence, trained immunity, cytokine and lipid mediator networks, immunometabolic reprogramming, neuroendocrine regulation, and repurposed drugs including metformin and statins. Importantly, we distinguish between evidence derived directly from TB models (in vitro, animal, and clinical studies) and evidence extrapolated from other diseases, highlighting knowledge gaps and areas requiring further investigation. We propose that future progress depends on evidence-based stratification of HDT candidates, rigorous clinical trial design, and a personalised approach that accounts for patient comorbidities and immune status. This review aims to provide a balanced framework for advancing HDT from bench to bedside in TB therapy.

articles.titulo: VZV reactivation, immune remodeling, and dementia risk.
articles.autores: Zhang L, Wu S, Quan Y, Yao W
articles.resumo_original: Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) is a highly dermatotropic and neurotropic α-herpesvirus that causes varicella (chickenpox) during primary infection, subsequently establishing lifelong latency, and reactivates to cause herpes zoster when host immunity declines or suppressed. Recent large-scale epidemiological studies consistently associate herpes zoster immunization, particularly with the recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV), with a significantly reduced risk of incident dementia. These findings have prompted a rigorous re-evaluation of the infectious etiology of progressive neurodegeneration. This review integrates the intersecting molecular mechanisms of VZV latency, localized ganglionic immunosenescence, and systemic inflammaging. We critically evaluate a synergistic VZV-HSV-1 amyloidogenic cascade, while explicitly addressing the biological limitations of extrapolating these transient interactions to human central nervous system (CNS) neuropathology. Furthermore, we propose the hypothesis that AS01B-induced trained immunity may contribute to neuroprotection. Therefore, this review provides insight for understanding the systemic consequences of chronic VZV infection and the impact of adjuvant-mediated immune remodeling in aging populations.

articles.titulo: Single-cell transcriptomics uncovers persistent hepatic immunometabolic remodeling following SARS-CoV-2 infection in obese hosts.
articles.autores: Qian W, Wei X, Park SJ, Garcia Diaz J, Comlekoglu T, Yu J, Sun J, Hahn YS
articles.resumo_original: SARS-CoV-2 infection affects multiple organs, and chronic post-viral tissue injury is often associated with persistent immune dysregulation. Obesity and related metabolic disorders are major risk factors for severe COVID-19 and post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC), including liver dysfunction. To define hepatic responses during post-acute infection, we studied lean and diet-induced obese mice at 7 and 28 days following infection with mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2. Compared with lean mice, obese mice exhibited persistent lung inflammation and fibrosis, along with liver injury characterized by increased lipid accumulation, cellular apoptosis, and metabolic dysfunction. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed obesity-associated alterations in hepatic immune and metabolic programs during post-acute infection. In particular, hepatic macrophages in obese mice showed sustained inflammatory and metabolic transcriptional alterations, while hepatocytes displayed altered programs associated with gluconeogenesis and lipid metabolism. Endothelial cells also exhibited persistent transcriptional changes linked to immune activation and prothrombotic pathways. These alterations remained evident at 28 days post-infection, suggesting incomplete restoration of immune and metabolic homeostasis in obese liver. Collectively, our findings reveal persistent obesity-associated hepatic immunometabolic remodeling following SARS-CoV-2 infection and identify cellular and molecular programs that may contribute to post-acute liver sequelae in metabolically compromised hosts.

articles.titulo: Immunometabolic reprogramming of macrophages and neutrophils in acute pancreatitis: from metabolic stress to amplification and endogenous braking.
articles.autores: Ai Y, Zhang L, Wei A, Dong J, Pang T, Zhang Y, Wu K, Yao S
articles.resumo_original: Acute pancreatitis (AP) progression involves both the initiating acinar injury and immune responses that sustain or contain subsequent damage. This review integrates evidence on metabolic regulation in macrophages and neutrophils to examine its links to inflammatory effectors, clearance, and tissue protection. Glycolytic regulation can support inflammatory activation, while non-AP neutrophil studies show how substrate allocation supports oxidant production and neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) release. Metabolite signaling also participates in macrophage efferocytosis, repair-associated responses, and tissue antioxidant defense. Contrasting lactate effects in acinar injury and macrophage repair indicate that metabolic changes must be interpreted through their effects on particular cells and functions. We propose an integrated amplification-braking framework that connects metabolically supported inflammatory effectors to continued generation of injury-derived stimuli, and clearance, antioxidant, and repair functions to damage containment. These functions can coexist without receiving equivalent metabolic support, and protective braking is distinct from generalized immunosuppression. Evidence differs across cells and experimental systems; metabolic regulation of inflammatory activation does not by itself establish metabolic control of NET-mediated injury in AP. The framework provides a basis for evaluating whether metabolic interventions can limit damaging activity while preserving protective functions, but it is not a validated clinical model. Pairing metabolic changes with specific cellular functions and subsequent injury is central to testing these relationships.

articles.titulo: Prophylactic Soraphen A Treatment Attenuates Western Diet-Exacerbated IMQ-Induced Psoriasiform Inflammation.
articles.autores: Kao YS, Kommoss KS, Bieler T, Godoy GJ, Lopez Krol A, Boukhallouk F, Kommoss FKF, Heide D, Kirsch SH, Müller R, Heikenwälder M, Sparwasser T
articles.resumo_original: Psoriasis is a T-cell-mediated inflammatory disease amplified by metabolic stress. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 (ACC1)-dependent fatty acid synthesis is required for IL-17-producing T cells. Here, we asked whether short-term systemic administration of soraphen A (SorA), a dual ACC1/2 inhibitor, modulates imiquimod (IMQ)-induced psoriasiform inflammation under normal diet (ND) and Western diet (WD) conditions. Female C57BL/6J mice were fed ND or WD for 12 weeks prior to daily intraperitoneal injections of SorA or vehicle for 10 days, followed by 5 days of topical IMQ to induce psoriasiform dermatitis. Disease severity was assessed by macroscopic, histological, transcriptional, and flow cytometric readouts. Prophylactic SorA administration had no measurable effect in ND-fed mice. In WD-fed mice, prophylactic SorA reduced erythema, back skin thickening, and epidermal hyperplasia, whereas scaling remained unchanged. Selected histological skin readouts were numerically lower, whereas the qPCR panel showed no statistically significant differences. In skin-draining lymph nodes, IL-17A+ CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell frequencies and numbers were significantly reduced, whereas γδT17 cells did not differ significantly. Hepatic steatosis scores were unchanged, but hepatic neutrophil infiltration was reduced. Under the present prophylactic regimen, systemic SorA administration was associated with modest attenuation of WD-exacerbated IMQ-induced psoriasiform inflammation. These findings support further preclinical evaluation of ACC-targeted immunometabolic interventions in metabolically aggravated psoriasiform inflammation.

articles.titulo: 7-(Chloroquinolin-4-yl) Sulfanyl Derivatives, Optimization of the Synthesis, In Silico ADMET Profiling Studies, and Evaluation of the Biological Activity Against Leishmania mexicana.
articles.autores: Gelvez A, Labrador-Fagúndez L, Stella BG, Rivero S, Ramirez Y, Vidal T, Martinez-Sotillo N, Suárez A, Chávez K, Ramírez H, Blanco Z, Gutiérrez J, Charris J, Benaim G
articles.resumo_original: Leishmaniasis is a parasitic human infection that constitutes a major global health challenge due to limited therapeutic options, toxicity, resistance, and high costs of the drugs approved as therapy. In this study, a group of 7-chloroquinoline derivatives (5-12) was synthesized via an optimized route and evaluated against the human parasite Leishmania mexicana. Compounds were fully characterized and showed favorable in silico ADME/Tox profiles, including high predicted gastrointestinal absorption (>93%), although limited solubility and potential hepatotoxicity were observed for several derivatives. Biological assays demonstrated significant antileishmanial activity. Interestingly, intracellular amastigote assays revealed nanomolar potency and very high selectivity index (SI), with compound 12 exhibiting IC50 = 2.5 nM (SI = 21.030) and compound 9 IC50 = 5.2 nM (SI = 7.384). Mechanistic studies demonstrated concentration-dependent mitochondrial membrane depolarization and acidocalcisome alkalinization. Since these two organelles are both involved in bioenergetics and in parasite intracellular Ca2+ homeostasis, the results support the notion that intracellular Ca2+ disruption is an essential target for different drug actions. Overall, these findings support a multitarget mechanism and position these quinoline derivatives as promising chemical scaffolds for the development of improved antileishmanial strategies.

articles.titulo: Presynaptic filopodia form kinapses and promote convective membrane flow to sustain synchronous neurotransmitter release.
articles.autores: Jain A, Dong R, Kroll J, Webster JF, Moss J, Bikbaev A, Ultanir SK, Gonzalez-Sulser A, Rosenmund C, Heine M, Liu J, Cousin MA, Ivanova D
articles.resumo_original: Synaptic plasticity is the principal mechanism by which neural circuits compute and adapt. Presynaptic plasticity is traditionally regarded as a transient adaptation of the synaptic vesicle fusion and recycling machinery, whereas the role of structural remodeling of synaptic boutons remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate a mechanical coupling between presynaptic structural remodeling and synaptic efficacy. We find that dynamic presynaptic filopodia emerge during active synaptic transmission and deform synaptic boutons while forming transient contacts with postsynaptic structures, which we term neuronal kinapses. Filopodia formation is activity dependent and occurs in intact circuits and human brain. Mechanistically, filopodial growth induces convective in-plane membrane flow toward the filopodium, accelerating release site clearance, a process associated with sustained release probability during repeated synaptic vesicle fusion. As a result, filopodia formation favors an increase in synchronous over asynchronous neurotransmitter release. These results indicate that presynaptic structural remodeling can alter the spatial organization of neurotransmission and, through the membrane flow it generates, modulate its temporal precision.

articles.titulo: Inhibiting apolipoprotein C3 alleviates ferroptosis and cell damage induced by Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
articles.autores: Liu Y, Yang X, Ni T, Zong J, Qian C, Wang X, Yu J
articles.resumo_original:
To explore the induction effect of Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) infection on ferroptosis and inflammatory response in human hepatoma cells (Hep3B) and the regulatory effect of apolipoprotein C3(APOC3) on ferroptosis sensitivity.
Hep3B hepatocytes (MOI=5, 10, 15) were infected with the wild standard strain of PA (PAO1) for 4 h, 8 h, and 12 h respectively, and the survival rate of cells under different infection concentrations and times was detected by CCK-8. The morphological changes of cells were observed under an inverted microscope to determine the infection conditions. After adding ferroptosis inhibitors or siRNA respectively to inhibit the expression of APOC3, lipid droplets were labeled using oil red O staining, and the formation of lipid droplets was observed under an inverted microscope. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) were detected using a fluorescent probe (DCFH-DA), and lipid peroxidation levels were detected using a microplate reader. The expression levels of Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptor α (PPARα), APOC3 and related inflammatory factors were detected by RT-qPCR. The protein expression levels of APOC3 and the ferroptosis-related proteins SLC7A11 and ACSL4 were evaluated by Western blotting. The morphological changes of mitochondria in cells were observed by transmission electron microscopy. The content of Fe2+ in cells was detected using a divalent iron ion probe.
With the increase of infection concentration and the extension of time, the survival rate of Hep3B cells significantly decreased after PAO1 infection, and the cell morphology gradually changed from spindle-shaped to round and accompanied by fragmentation. The number of red lipid droplets within the cells increased with the increase of the bacterial load. The fluorescence intensity of ROS was enhanced. The expression of PPARα mRNA was down-regulated and the expression of APOC3 mRNA was up-regulated. The volume of mitochondria decreased, the membrane density increased, and the cristae were reduced or even disappeared. Western blotting further confirmed the changes in APOC3 protein expression and ferroptosis-related proteins, including SLC7A11 and ACSL4, following PAO1 infection and APOC3 knockdown. The intracellular lipid peroxidation level was significantly increased. Compared with the control group, the levels of IL-6 and TNF-α significantly increased after PA infection. After inhibiting the expression of APOC3, the expression level of ROS decreased, lipid peroxidation reduced, the number of lipid droplets decreased, the content of Fe2+ decreased, mitochondrial damage decreased, and the expression of ferroptosis-related factors decreased.
After the action of PA, cell activity significantly decreased, intracellular ROS generation increased, and intracellular lipid peroxidation was enhanced, leading to cell damage and death. Meanwhile, APOC3, as a key downstream target of PPARα, PA promotes the generation of APOC3 by inhibiting the expression of PPARα, and APOC3 reduces the hydrolysis of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins (TRL), thereby promoting lipid droplet formation. It causes the accumulation of lipids within cells. However, the continuous inhibitionof APOC3 can reverse this effect. That is, after PA infects cells, it can promote the increase of APOC3 expression, leading to lipid metabolism disorders, and APOC3 plays a promoting role in the process of PA promoting ferroptosis in cells.

articles.titulo: Sustainable synthesis of metallic nanoparticles and their potential biotechnological applications.
articles.autores: Ugale SV, Gaikwad SC, Bankar AV, Nawani N
articles.resumo_original: Nanotechnology has emerged as a vital interdisciplinary field with applications in medicine, biotechnology, environmental remediation, agriculture, energy, and advanced materials. Metallic nanoparticles (NPs), typically ranging from 1 to 100 nm, have distinctive physicochemical characteristics, including small size, a high surface-area-to-volume ratio, surface reactivity, and tunable electronic properties. Although conventional physical and chemical methods can effectively control nanoparticle (NP) composition and morphology, they may require high energy inputs, specialized equipment, or potentially toxic reagents. Therefore, biological synthesis strategies using plants, microorganisms, and biologically derived molecules have received much attention as alternative approaches for metallic NP synthesis.This review critically evaluates conventional, biological, and hybrid strategies for synthesizing metallic NPS, with particular emphasis on silver (Ag), copper (Cu), and silver-copper (Ag-Cu) bimetallic nanomaterials. The review also discusses NP's characterization methods, including UV-Visible (UV-Vis) spectroscopy, Electron microscopy (EM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), Dynamic light scattering (DLS), zeta-potential analysis, and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), while emphasizing the limitations of interpreting any single technique in isolation. This work highlights the transition from laboratory-scale green synthesis to reproducible, scalable nanomanufacturing, including challenges associated with batch-to-batch reproducibility, biological-feedstock variability, purification, process control, safety, toxicity, and life-cycle sustainability. Finally, the review highlights the diverse biotechnological applications of metallic NPs in antimicrobial systems, diagnostics, drug delivery, agriculture, environmental remediation, and related industrial sectors. Overall, the review argues that biological synthesis methods should not automatically be regarded as sustainable. Instead, assess their advantages by integrating material performance, process efficiency, reproducibility, scalability, safety, and environmental impact.

articles.titulo: Biochar-immobilised phosphate-solubilising bacteria enhance soil available phosphorus by affecting phosphorus fraction transformation and phosphorus-acquiring microbiota.
articles.autores: Zhou L, Peng L, Rousk J, Deng H, Mu L, Wang Z, Dai W, Gao M
articles.resumo_original: Phosphate-solubilising bacteria (PSB) play an important role in phosphorus (P) transformation and plant P uptake. However, their effectiveness is often limited by environmental instability and soil poor survival. Biochar has been proposed as a suitable carrier for microbial immobilisation; however, the effects of biochar-immobilised PSB on soil P fractions and the microbial mechanisms underlying P transformation remain unclear. In this study, we developed a biochar-immobilised PSB using Klebsiella sp. N107 and assessed its effects on soil P availability, P fraction transformation, and microbial processes regulating P cycling. A pot experiment was conducted: no fertilisation, conventional fertilisation (NPK), NPK + pristine biochar (NPKB), NPK + PSB (NPKP), and NPK + biochar-immobilised PSB (NPKBP). Soil properties, P fractions, organic acids, enzyme activities, and metagenomic characteristics were analysed. Compared with NPKB and NPKP, NPKBP enhanced plant P uptake and soil available P. It also increased labile P fractions, organic acid concentrations, and the activities of P acquiring enzymes. Genes associated with P transport (pit, ugpB, ugpQ, and ugpE), polyphosphate degradation (ppk1 and ppk2), organic P mineralisation (phoA and phoD), and inorganic P solubilisation (gcd, ppa, and ppx) were upregulated. P acquiring taxa, including Sphingomonas, Gaiella, and Bradyrhizobium, were enriched and contributed functionally to P cycling. Overall, biochar-immobilised PSB improved soil P availability by promoting P fraction transformation and restructuring microbial communities involved in P cycling. Soil pH, organic acids, and available nitrogen were identified as key drivers of these processes, highlighting the potential of biochar-immobilised PSB to improve soil P utilisation and management.

articles.titulo: Pressure Engineering through Silica Nanoconfinement for Melting Point Elevation of Gold Nanoparticles.
articles.autores: Choi CW, Choi JH, Kim GY, Lee IS, Choi SY
articles.resumo_original: Au nanoparticles (NPs) are inherently thermally unstable at elevated temperatures because their large surface-to-volume ratio promotes melting, migration, and coalescence. Here, we demonstrate that silica (SiO2) nanoconfinement thermodynamically elevates the melting point (Tm) of Au NPs through confinement-induced compressive pressure. Atomic-resolution in situ heating scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) combined with local Fourier crystallinity mapping reveals that bare Au NPs lose crystallinity at 1,000 °C, whereas SiO2-encapsulated Au cores (Au@SiO2) remain crystalline. Accordingly, in situ heating TEM shows bare Au NPs progressively merge while Au@SiO2 remain structurally isolated. Temperature-dependent lattice-parameter measurements reveal significantly suppressed thermal expansion of confined Au cores, corresponding to an estimated compressive stress of 4-5 GPa. Finite-element simulations support this estimate, showing that SiO2 shell shrinkage generates several-GPa core pressure, with thicker shells producing higher pressure and greater Tm elevation. These findings establish nanoconfinement-induced pressure as a general thermomechanical strategy for stabilizing metallic NPs under extreme thermal environments.

articles.titulo: Dual-Phosphorylated Pumpkin Seed Protein Pickering Emulsions: Structural Evolution, Interfacial Regulation, and Coffee Creamer Application Quality.
articles.revista: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
articles.autores: Huang J, Wang D, Ruan Z, Xu H, Yang Z, Chen J
articles.resumo_original: Pumpkin seed protein (PSP) was modified with sodium tripolyphosphate (STP) and sodium trimetaphosphate (STMP) to improve Pickering emulsions. Phosphorylation increased with STMP content but plateaued at high ratios. Mass spectrometry identified phosphorylated Ser and Thr residues, while 31P NMR indicated multiple phosphorus environments. Modification altered protein conformation and surface charge, reduced particle size, and improved dispersion without major subunit degradation. Although emulsifying activity decreased, emulsion stability increased; mixed-phosphate treatments generally produced finer droplets and better resistance to centrifugal destabilization than single-phosphate treatments. A 4:1 STP/STMP ratio combined small droplet size with favorable wettability and interfacial adsorption, whereas higher STMP content did not consistently improve overall performance. In coffee beverages, increasing emulsion incorporation intensified phase separation and altered color and flavor. At a 1:9 emulsion-to-coffee ratio, phosphorylated PSP emulsion improved perceived body and smoothness while retaining coffee aroma, outperforming commercial creamer in balance and supporting its potential use as a plant-based food.

articles.titulo: Design, Characterization and In Vivo Evaluation of Rifaximin-Loaded Chitosan Nanoparticles for Potential Colonic Drug Delivery in Irritable Bowel Syndrome.
articles.autores: Deljavan Ghodrati A, Comoglu T
articles.resumo_original: This study aimed to develop rifaximin (RFX) loaded chitosan (CS)-tripolyphosphate (TPP) nanoparticles for potential colonic delivery as a drug delivery system for the management of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Nanoparticles were prepared using the ionotropic gelation method and optimized by varying stirring speed, TPP concentration, and polymer-to-drug ratio. The optimized formulation (F41) exhibited a particle size of 262.4 ± 24.3 nm, a polydispersity index (PDI) of 0.389 ± 0.033, a zeta potential of + 9.91 ± 0.94 mV, and an encapsulation efficiency (EE%) of 94.75 ± 0.04%. In vitro release studies demonstrated nearly complete drug release within 36 h, which was faster compared to other formulations (52-64 h). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) confirmed spherical morphology, while differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) analyses indicated successful drug encapsulation without chemical interaction. In vivo evaluation using a chronic restraint stress (CRS) induced IBS model showed that F41 significantly improved physiological parameters, including reduced fecal water content (20.655 ± 23.494%), increased body weight gain (22.716 ± 3.903%), and a decreased disease activity index (p < 0.05). These findings indicate that, the optimized nanoparticle system demonstrated favorable physicochemical properties, sustained drug release, and improved therapeutic outcomes. Owing to the cationic nature of CS, the system may also provide enhanced interaction with colonic mucus, potentially contributing to prolonged local residence. These findings suggest that the developed formulation represents promising approach for potential colonic delivery of RFX in IBS management; however, further studies are required to directly evaluate its mucoadhesive properties and underlying mechanisms.

articles.titulo: Electrostatic multipolar probe-forming objective lens for FIB.
articles.autores: Berdou-Durrieu L, Mellier JB, Fay JB, Salord O, Reveillard M, Warot-Fonrose B, Viteau M, Houdellier F
articles.resumo_original: This paper explores the possibility of using a system of four aligned electrostatic quadrupoles, also known as Russian quadruplet, as an objective lens for a Focused Ion Beam (FIB). The system has been designed compact to be fitted onto standard FIB columns installed in dual beam systems. Each quadrupole has been designed to allow for simple mechanical assembly, whilst retaining the ability to generate an octopole field self-centered with the main quadrupole field by polarizing the ground apertures surrounding the main electrodes. The goal of this additional octopole field will be to compensate for strong aperture aberrations. The performance of this new probe-forming multipole objective lens has been investigated by spot milling a silicon sample's surface using both LMIS and plasma sources. Probe-forming properties and beam shape affected by aperture aberrations of the new Russian quadruplet objective lens are then observed by Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) images and compared with standard spots observed using conventional rotational symmetric einzel lens. Using an LMIS source, we were able to focus spots with sizes, depending on the current range, at least equivalent to those obtained with conventional optics, while maintaining a working distance more than three times greater. In particular, at low currents in the tens-of-picoampere range, spot diameters of 200 nanometers were achieved, which are half the size of conventional spots. At high currents in the hundred-of-nanoamperes range, spot diameters in the micrometer range were achieved. The results obtained with a plasma source made it possible to generate spots in the tens-of-micrometers range at high currents, while maintaining the advantage of the large working distance. However, for long etching times in the hundred of seconds, a long "evanescent line" is observed along one direction. We will discuss its origin and propose ways to correct this artifact. Finally a first milling application using focused ion lines is also presented at the end of this work.

articles.titulo: Molecular Packaging, Liquid-Crystalline Order, and Three-Dimensional Architecture of Dinoflagellate Chromosomes.
articles.autores: Chung JM, Suzaki T, Fukuda Y, Song C
articles.resumo_original: Many dinoflagellates package exceptionally large nuclear genomes within the dinokaryon, a nucleus that departs from conventional eukaryotic patterns of chromosome condensation, DNA packaging, and mitosis. Their chromosomes remain visibly condensed through most or all of the cell cycle. In many core dinoflagellates, DNA exhibits cholesteric liquid-crystalline order, while canonical nucleosomal chromatin does not serve as the dominant structural framework. This review synthesizes current evidence on dinoflagellate chromosome organization, spanning molecular packaging mechanisms and three-dimensional nuclear architecture. Dinoflagellates are histone-poor rather than histone-free: divergent core histones persist at low abundance, whereas HCc/MBNP-type proteins can be highly abundant in some species, with additional contributions from dinoflagellate viral nucleoproteins, divalent cations, RNA-associated factors, and modified DNA bases. Classical electron microscopy revealed nested arch patterns consistent with cholesteric order and inspired spiral, double-helical, and toroidal chromonema models, although molecular-resolution support remains lacking and fixation-sensitive features require caution. Recent volume electron microscopy and chromosome-conformation studies are revising chromosome counts and nuclear organization. Each of four reconstructed Oxyrrhis marina nuclei contained 398-405 physically segmented chromosome bodies, focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) reconstruction of a Prorocentrum cordatum CCMP 1329 nucleus resolved 62 tightly packed chromosome bodies together with an organized nucleolus and clustered nuclear pores, and high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) studies in Symbiodiniaceae revealed chromosome-scale scaffolds and transcription-dependent domains. Integrating standardized volume electron microscopy, chromosome-scale genomics, cryo-electron tomography, and biochemical reconstitution should connect molecular packaging to whole-nucleus architecture and improve understanding of ecologically important microbial eukaryotes.

articles.titulo: Self-adaptive layered oxide cathodes driven by charge reconfiguration for sodium-ion batteries.
articles.autores: Li JY, Guo Y, Wang X, Pang WK, Hu HY, Zhu YF, Chen D, Liu XY, Gu QF, Johannessen B, Zheng X, Sun Y, Cheng S, Yuan Y, Wu C, Wang JZ, Dou SX, Xiao Y
articles.resumo_original: Layered oxide cathodes have attracted worldwide attention due to environmentally friendliness, structural diversity, and economic benefits. However, poor long-term cycling and unsatisfactory rate performance hinder the practical application. Hence, an oxide cathode with self-adaptive volume has been designed, achieving stable capacity retention of 82% after 1000 cycles at 2 C. The enhanced long-term performance is attributed to its dynamically adjustable volume reducing the acceleration of stress, enabled by a tunable interlayer distance that expands at the beginning of the charging process and then compresses at the highest voltage. Uniform electric field distribution is depicted by 4-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy showing even Coulombic interactions between the oxide layers leading to high mechanical integrity. Such self-adaptable behavior originates from the reduced repulsive force between interlayered oxygen due to the charge reconfiguration of intralayer oxygen and transition metal ions. Additionally, the charge compensation behavior is detected by in situ X-ray absorption spectra, which would be beneficial to high-rate performance. The self-adaptive volume change driven by charge reconfiguration provides a pathway toward durable materials for sustainable sodium-ion energy storage.

articles.titulo: Ablation of Tnfr1 Gene Impairs Enamel Surface Microhardness and Mineral Composition in Mice.
articles.revista: The International journal of developmental biology
articles.autores: Gonçalves JL, Almeida-Júnior LA, Arnez MFM, Galo R, Queiroz AM, Carvalho FK, Paula-Silva FWG
articles.resumo_original: While the immune response is increasingly suspected to play a role in dental enamel defects, the specific pathways involved remain unclear. This study investigated the effects of Tnfrsf1a (TNF receptor superfamily member 1A) gene ablation on amelogenesis and enamel biomineralization. Male Tnfrsf1a knockout (Tnfrsf1a-/-) and wild-type (C57BL/6) mice (n = 6 per group) were evaluated. Lower incisors were analyzed using visual photography, micro-computed tomography (microCT), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), surface microhardness testing, and energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) spectroscopy. Protein expression of MMP20, RUNX2, and AMBN was assessed via immunohistochemistry, while in situ zymography quantified MMP gelatinolytic activity. Gene expression was analyzed using RT-qPCR. Tnfrsf1a-/- mice exhibited no macroscopic opacities, though incisors displayed a distinct whitish coloration. While microCT and SEM revealed no significant differences in enamel volume, or prism ultrastructure, the enamel of Tnfrsf1a-/- mice showed significantly lower calcium and phosphorus content and reduced surface microhardness. Molecular analysis revealed that the Ambn gene was significantly upregulated during both the secretion and maturation stages in Tnfrsf1a-/- mice compared to wild-type controls. Ablation of Tnfrsf1a results in enamel color change in mice characterized by altered mineral composition, reduced mechanical hardness, and dysregulated Ambn expression. These findings suggest that TNF signaling acts as a critical modulator during amelogenesis and is essential for achieving the final mineral quality of dental enamel.

articles.titulo: A conserved insect transcobalamin-like gene is associated with vitamin B12-related functions in the silkworm Bombyx mori.
articles.autores: Xiang JH, Wu Y, Xie QH, Chen BZ, Yi MY, Li FY, Tong XL, Feng QL, Wang M, Xiang H
articles.resumo_original: Vitamin B12 (VB12, cobalamin) is delivered by transcobalamin-dependent pathways in mammals, but comparable host-encoded factors and functions in insects remain unclear. Here we identify a single transcobalamin-like gene in the silkworm Bombyx mori ( Bmtcn) and detect homologs across diverse insect orders. Structure prediction and docking suggest that insect transcobalamin (TCN)-like proteins retain a conserved fold and a pocket compatible with cobalamin binding, although direct biochemical validation remains needed. Bmtcn expression is enriched in the head and is detectable across neuronal and glial populations, implicating the nervous system as a potential site of cobalamin handling and/or demand. Bmtcn loss-of-function mutants accumulate homocysteine, display behavioral abnormalities, and show brain-associated phenotypes. Head transcriptomics reveals coordinated changes consistent with perturbed folate-one-carbon metabolism and broad remodeling of core cellular programs alongside stress-associated responses in the mutants. Because insects lack canonical cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase, these findings suggest that cobalamin may act through alternative metabolic and/or signaling routes. Together, our results implicate a conserved insect transcobalamin-like component in vitamin B12-linked physiology and B. mori as a tractable system for mechanistic dissection.

articles.titulo: Glutamate receptor composition at Drosophila neuromuscular junctions depends on developmental stage and muscle identity.
articles.autores: Sustar A, Qiu C, Xiong Y, Dickman DK, Tuthill JC
articles.resumo_original: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) of larval Drosophila is widely used for studying synaptic transmission. Larval body wall muscles express five ionotropic glutamate receptor (iGluR) subunits that assemble into two tetrameric complexes, with subunit composition determining the strength and plasticity of synaptic transmission. Because NMJ function has been extensively characterized in larvae, it has commonly been assumed that adult fly NMJs share this molecular composition, despite substantial differences between life stages. Here, we systematically compare glutamate receptor expression across larval and adult Drosophila muscles. We find that adult leg and flight muscles exhibit different iGluR expression than larvae, lacking expression of several receptors previously considered essential. Adjacent muscles within the adult femur express distinct iGluRs, suggesting specialization of flexor and extensor muscles. Finally, the glutamate-gated chloride channel (GluClα) is expressed extrasynaptically in adult but not larval muscle fibers. Our results reveal unexpected heterogeneity in glutamate receptor expression across muscles and developmental stages, demonstrating the need for muscle-specific analyses in flies and other animals.

articles.titulo: Advances in research on the regulation of honey bee odor and chemical communication by symbiotic microorganisms.
articles.autores: Chen YJ, Wang YC, Pang YT, Fang RC, Zhang J, Ke XH, Li JJ, Zhang LS, Yang S, Guo J, Miao CH
articles.resumo_original: Because honey bees are key pollinators in terrestrial ecosystems, they are highly sensitive to environmental changes, and colony survival serves as a reliable indicator of environmental conditions. Insect symbiotic microorganisms regulate host chemical communication through multiple pathways, thereby playing critical roles in pheromone synthesis, olfactory perception, and social behavior modulation. However, a systematic review of the potential regulatory mechanisms by which symbiotic microorganisms influence chemical communication in honey bees is still lacking. Here, we synthesize domestic and international research to assess the compositions of symbiotic microorganisms in honey bees, as well as the mechanisms of pheromone release, perception, and function. Furthermore, drawing on specific experimental cases, we discuss how honey bee symbionts modulate host sensitivity to chemical signals and consequently affect host social behavior through multiple routes. These pathways are involved in regulating odorant-binding protein or odorant receptor expression and nervous system function, altering cuticular hydrocarbon profiles, modulating olfactory memory, and mediating immune signaling. This review further explores the interplay between symbiotic microorganisms and the release and reception of chemical signals in honey bees, thereby providing a solid foundation for the conservation of endangered pollinating insects.

articles.titulo: Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator for fly walking.
articles.autores: Pugliese SM, Chou GM, Abe ETT, Turcu D, Lancaster JK, Tuthill JC, Brunton BW
